The forum was moderated by LWV co-president Nancy Beninati. articles.text: Measure TT, the real property transfer tax, will appear on the November 3 municipal ballot alongside Measure UU. Unlike Measure UU, Measure TT only requires a simple majority vote. If adopted by voters, Measure TT would increase the existing real property conveyance tax from the existing rate of $13 per $1,000 of transfer price, to $17.50 per $1,000 of transfer price. Like the current Real Property Transfer Tax, the increase being put before the voters in Measure TT, would be a general tax. “The council has stated its intention to put increased revenues from this tax, if approved, towards facilities maintenance,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand explained. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee has recommended that the city devote increased funding to facilities maintenance, which was included in their report to city council on June 15, 2020. The committee recommended an increase in the Real Property Transfer Tax to fund facilities maintenance. Funds garnered from the general tax and its proceeds are deposited in the city’s general fund. This fund is used for the general operations of Piedmont. “To catch up on the City’s facilities maintenance backlog, the council generally makes a transfer from the General fund to the Facilities Maintenance Fund each budget year,” Lillevand said. articles.text: My husband and I have been exploring Piedmont streets on foot as much as possible while the COVID-19 travel restrictions are in force. We’ve enjoyed acquainting ourselves with streets we’d previously only traversed by car. This morning we walked along Highland to Blair, where we turned left to continue on our way. As we crossed Oakland Ave., we were startled by a white van traveling down Oakland Avenue from above Blair. We’d been watching for traffic, so we weren’t in any danger, but as we continued up Blair, we saw two girls on a bike (a young teenager on the seat and a slightly younger girl behind her) coasting down Blair toward Oakland and picking up speed on the steep decline. They shrieked as they approached the corner of Blair and Oakland, then blew through the stop sign and turned left (uphill) to slow down. It terrified me to imagine what might have happened if the girls had reached the corner a minute or two earlier, at the same time that the van arrived. Visibility is poor, and it’s unlikely that they or the van could have avoided a collision. My older son and his friends used to ride their skateboards down some of Piedmont’s steepest streets, looking for a thrill and feeling invincible. They survived to terrify us years later with tales of their exploits. I can only hope today’s bike riders are equally as lucky. –Karen Mead
articles.title: Teens on bikes – a cautionary tale

articles.text: Mayor All Piedmont households recently received a letter from me asking for a Yes vote on Measure TT; the proposal to increase the Real Property Transfer Tax (“Transfer Tax”). It is on the ballot in the November 3 election. I want to highlight several important points. For almost a decade, the City Council has taken constructive steps to improve the City’s financial position by controlling costs and addressing long-term liabilities. The City Council and staff have been disciplined in managing resources to ensure that our high-quality services can be sustained and that a strategy is in place to address long-term financial challenges. The Council has a strong record of cautious financial management and will continue to carefully manage the City’s resources. The City’s aging infrastructure is the next challenge. The proposed increase in the Transfer Tax is focused on that issue. This increase will provide vital funding and help take on that challenge: The City can pave more streets, repair more sidewalks, improve park maintenance, and better address our aging city facilities. Piedmont voters first approved the Transfer Tax in 1968. In 1993, voters approved an increase to $13.00 per $1,000 of the sales price of homes when sold. Piedmont’s rate has remained unchanged for the past 27 years For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. and is significantly lower than comparable rates in Berkeley and Oakland. Measure TT would increase the tax to $17.50 per $1,000 of sales price. The tax is assessed only when a property is bought or sold and impacts relatively few residents each year. It’s important to keep in mind that the Transfer Tax is one of the few ways Piedmont can raise additional funds to address our aging infrastructure. Unlike Berkeley and Oakland, Piedmont does not have a robust commercial or industrial tax base. My eight years of volunteer service to the City ends in early December. I could not be more impressed by the response of our staff and our residents to the unprecedented events and challenges we have faced this year. I have never been prouder to serve as Mayor of Piedmont. I know you believe in the bright future of our community as much as I do, and I urge you to Vote Yes on both Measures TT and UU.
articles.title: Why Measure TT is vital to Piedmont’s future

articles.text: Editor: The day after I mailed my ballot home from Paris, I learned something that I had not noticed from my too-casual reading of Prop. 19. Voters need to read it carefully all the way through, as deep within it is a stowaway provision. Most voters won’t notice or understand its impact. It is a provision that should have been presented as a stand-alone proposition. Under present law a person may inherit a residence from his or her parents, including a rental residence, and the transfer of title does not have any tax consequences. The transfer of title does not trigger a reassessment of the property’s value to present market value. Prop. 19 changes this and provides that the transfer of title does trigger a reassessment of the property to present market value. This means that a house bought in 1978 for $60,000 and now taxed at $1600 a year will, when inherited, be taxed based on its present value, say $800,000, and the annual tax will increase to something well over $8000. This provision deserves to be considered on its own merits and not smuggled in with the other, more wholesome, provisions of Prop 19. –Michael A. articles.text: Editor: Like many Piedmonters, we know there are so many good reasons to re-elect Jennifer Cavenaugh to City Council. We’ve been lucky enough to see Jen in action as a leader, a mentor and a friend. Jen has the experience, intelligence and heart to lead our city in making smart choices that bring us all closer together. She takes an inclusive and datadriven approach to ensure Piedmont serves the needs of the entire community. In addition to her four years on the Piedmont City Council, Jen led the Rec. Department Community Outreach Program, served as President of the Piedmont Language School and on the Parent Club Boards for Beach, PMS and PHS. In all of these roles, she has reached out to a wide range of stakeholders to develop programs and solutions that meet the needs of the entire community. Jen’s leadership has resulted in the launch of new Rec. Department programs for adults and teens, including the innovative Healthy Relationships program. She has helped the community tackle complex issues like upgrading our pool facilities through Measure UU and engage in important conversations about race by organizing the Let’s Talk program. She’s also encouraged countless other Piedmonters to join a committee, advocate for an idea or run for office. In each of these instances, Jen has taken the time to inform and educate herself, reach out to a wide range of people for input and lead in a way that encourages others to rally around a common goal. We trust Jen to serve our community with integrity, smarts, passion and good judgment. We hope all Piedmonters vote and will join us in supporting Jen Cavenaugh for another term. –Rani and Nick Batra
articles.title: Many reasons to re-elect Jen Cavenaugh

A vote for Conna is a vote for us all. –Tami & Mark Becker and Family
articles.title: A family in support of Conna McCarthy

articles.text: Editor: The teachers of Piedmont Unified School District are excited to share their support for Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen for School Board. After interviews with each candidate, deliberations, and considerations about the current needs of our students, we believe that Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are the best candidates to meet the needs of our school community. Substantial changes to the educational and social landscape mean that we need candidates who will guide us into the future. These changes include renewed recognition of issues concerning equity, commitment to differences in learning, and an understanding that the students of today will need to navigate new terrain regarding technology, social interactions, environment, career, and more. Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are candidates for positive change; they will bring important new perspectives to our School Board leadership. We are grateful that the current School Board has taken many important steps in terms of social justice and equity, and we believe these candidates will help take this work to the next level. Veronica Anderson Thigpen brings a wealth of experience as a journalist writing about educational policy and as an educational consultant on issues of equity in education. Jason Kelley brings a background in law, as well as broad experience and knowledge of Piedmont schools and issues concerning Special Education. Through their work on local committees, volunteerism, and experience as Piedmont parents, each has demonstrated a commitment and love for Piedmont schools. Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen will build bridges between teachers, students, and families that will form the basis for strong productive partnerships. Most importantly, as educational professionals, we are confident that they will be a positive force in the lives of our students. Support our students. Vote for Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen. Gabe Kessler is President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers.
articles.title: Teachers union in support of Kelley, Thigpen

articles.text: Editor: When Veronica Anderson Thigpen told me she was running for Piedmont School Board, I cried with joy. Since the first time I met her, she has taken an interest in my thoughts and opinions. Talking with her, I truly felt seen and heard. And speaking with other students in Piedmont, I’ve come to learn I am not an exception. Veronica values all student voices. While she brings a great resume as an educator, journalist, scholar, parent and community leader, what I love most about her is how she makes young people feel included and valued. That is critical to our school board’s mission to be more inclusive. I am reaching out to parents, grandparents and the entire Piedmont community on her behalf. Some of us are too young to vote. Keep us in your heart when you complete your ballot. Vote for the candidate who sees and listens to us — Veronica Anderson Thigpen for school board. –Casey Hidekawa PHS Class of 2019 Stanford Class of 2023
articles.title: Thigpen – paying attention to voices of students

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to enthusiastically support Jen Cavenaugh’s re-election to City Council. I have had the privilege of getting to know Jen through my work as co-chair of the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) Housing/Zoning committee and other community causes. Jen is exactly the kind of intelligent, committed, progressive leader our city needs. In the time I’ve known Jen, I have consistently been impressed by her combination of knowledge, diplomatic skill, perseverance, attention to detail, and responsiveness to constituents. When taking on complex issues such as state and local housing policy, policing, and physical and financial planning for our city’s future, Jen consistently does her research, asks smart and well-informed questions, communicates effectively, and follows through with concrete actions.
articles.title: Cavenaugh a supporter of progressive causes

articles.text: In the summer of 1998, a small group of Piedmont high school parents frustrated by the lack of local coverage after the local paper had been sold got together with a plan. Meeting in a neighbor’s house with a large map of the city tacked onto the wall, they laid out the front page of what would become the Piedmont Post. Gray Cathrall, then a part-time sports writer, sent a letter to some 300 people – pretty much everyone he knew in town – inviting them to become subscribers and underwriters of a new paper, the Piedmont Post. Within four weeks, he raised three times what he needed to launch and sustain the paper for a half year. The first issue was delivered to homes through the city on October 20. It was an instant hit: when Gray, the Post’s publisher and editor, came by the high school office to drop off some copies, he saw scores of high schoolers reading the paper in the courtyard. “Any time we can get kids to sit down and read the newspaper, we’ve done something right,” he said later. This week, the Piedmont Post celebrates its 22nd anniversary, a stunning achievement in the world where not a day goes by without the news of another publication in the U.S. folding. No longer a shoestring operation, the paper has a vibrant staff of reporters, photographers, graphic designers, production specialists, columnists, and reviewers. Piedmont residents still make up a healthy portion of financial support along with advertising, which, in a small community with very little commerce, remains remarkable “This is a town that is passionate about having a paper,” said Cathrall. In its early days, the Post made a few decisions by which it abides today. The paper is content-heavy, with prominent space given to residents’ opinions, local news and politics, school matters and sports. It also features PPD Blue, an unedited log from the Piedmont Police Department whose hilarious entries make siblings fight for the right to read the paper first. Unusual for most local papers, it maintains a wide-ranging performing arts section, with live reviews of Bay Area theaters, symphony, opera and regional music organizations. Delivered every Wednesday by an army of primarily middle school-aged students, the Post provides as close to real-time news coverage as is possible with a weekly newspaper. Over the years it has shone the spotlight on countless important, sometimes controversial town matters, challenging city and school administration on staffing, budget, bond issue decisions. The paper consistently provided space for debate on topics from cellphone tower installations to community pool repairs, bringing forth a diversity of voices. It also has made a point of encouraging students to express themselves in print. Some are seen in print early. The current high school senior class president made her writing debut as a fourth grader when the paper published her petition to the City Council to reverse the candy throwing ban at the town’s Fourth of July Parade. The Post is also a chronicler of our lives in this hilly town by the bay. At home, many families have thick scrapbooks with Post’s cutouts that track the lives of their children, through sports teams, school activities and rallies, and even graduation speeches. Some of the lucky ones even show up in the popular where in the World Are We? photo feature (when they remember to send a photo from their latest vacation destination). For many, reading the paper on Wednesday nights has become a ritual. In the world that’s increasingly slipping into a myriad of disjointed silos, the Post, with its wall-to-wall coverage of the town and its inhabitants, reminds us we’re members of the community, not just residents. The Post’s value has come into an even sharper relief now, when the COVID pandemic has ruptured connections through shelter-in-place orders, school closures and cancellations of the activities that make the fabric of this town: sports tournaments, school dances, festivals, concerts. In these difficult times, the Post has lent its pages to support for local businesses fighting for survival, to Piedmonters away from home journaling their experience, as well as to throwbacks of past sports events as points of reference. It continues to be a paragon of non-politicized free speech, of important information about all things local, and a vehicle for all of us to stay together. Reflecting on the paper’s success, Gray, the Post’s towering 6’2” presence, is humble. “We were not really trying to do anything clever or catchy, but answering the question: Does this make sense for the residents of the community? It’s their paper. We just publish it.” Lic. No. 702138 Request a Virtual or On-Site Quote

articles.text: The Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee, under the auspices of Piedmont City Council, held its first public meeting on October 13. The newly formed committee is tasked with implementing a safe streets master plan, and immediately dug in with an initial meeting lasting three hours. Six years ago, on November 3, 2014, the city council unanimously adopted the Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan, with the intent of improving conditions for pedestrians and cyclists throughout the city. The master plan pays special attention to the needs of school children, because much of the walking and biking activity in Piedmont consists of children going to and from school. For these reasons the process was planned from the beginning to include a “Safe Routes to School” component. Its objective was to incorporate final recommendations in the master plan for improvements that will encourage more young residents to walk and bike to school, rather than drive or be taken in a carpool. The plan builds on other local planning efforts, particularly the city’s general plan, the American with Disabilities Act Rightof-Way Transition Plan, Climate Action Plan and Complete Streets policy. One example of this type of project is the Craig Avenue and Highland Avenue Crosswalk Enhancement (bulb-out) that was completed as part of the 2019 Paving Project and was identified in the master plan. There are many residual projects that will fall under the guidance of the committee. These include crosswalk enhancements at Oakland and Grand Avenue, Moraga and Highland Avenue, Oakland and Hillside Avenue, and Hampton Road and La Salle Avenue. The committee will also consider reconfiguration of the intersection at the corporation yard at Moraga Avenue and Red Rock Road, and various improvements to Magnolia Avenue and Highland Avenue. Enhanced street crossings are considered a high-priority project for the committee. To address safety concerns, the aforementioned intersections would feature a range of improvements, including striped crosswalks, sidewalk bulb-outs or extensions, advanced yield or stop lines, flashing crossing signs, pedestrian islands, and signage. It is estimated that the safer streets project will last less than a year, concluding in July 2021. The project will include public outreach. The committee includes Hugh Louch, Katie DeWitt, Sofia Barandiaran, Eugene Brown, Jr., Brett Hondorp, Tom Reicher, Kristin Robrock and students Audrey Edel, Piedmont senior class president, and Siddarth Bhatia, a freshman. Gopika Nair from the city staff will be the liaison. At the first meeting committee members chose Louch as Chair and DeWitt as Vice Chair. The committee is conducting a community needs assessment to determine what changes need to be made to the 2014 master plan. The committee will then present the report to the Planning Commission and City Council in the near future. Here are the simple steps for purchasing a beautiful tree: 1. articles.text: Each year the Grants Committee of the Piedmont Education Foundation meets multiple times to determine the best recommendations for the use of funds raised through the Giving Campaign and other PEF fundraising efforts. The Grants Committee is led by PEF board members and includes representatives from Parents Clubs, Support Groups, the PUSD administration, and other community members. Fighting uncertainty: What parents can do By Nina Meehan Uncertainty. Will the kids actually go back to school? Once they are back, will they be able to stay in school? What will flu season look like? Will working from home become our new normal? These questions and so many more have become a drumbeat in our lives – a constant thump that never really leaves us. We adults have all learned to live with it, perhaps normalizing or quieting it with the hectic balance of home-school, work, household and community obligations. But, for our small people, whose ears are more sensitive than ours, this drumbeat of uncertainty may feel like the whole percussion section. So what’s a parent to do? There really is no end in sight right now, and our kids need to silence those cymbals so that they can learn, grow and thrive. I know for my family, when the pandemic hit we suddenly had more screen time enter our lives than ever before. I’m pretty sure we’re not alone in that. And now, eight months into this crisis, I’d really like to return to a more normal balance, but my energy is fast becoming depleted. I don’t know any parent right now who has the bandwidth for a multi-day project recreating the Jurassic period by turning our bedroom into a prehistoric jungles cape using all recycled and eco-friendly materials. But we can focus on what I like to think of as micro-moments of creativity – small engagements, maybe just once a day, that give us all a moment of connection and joy. Maybe we can sit with our kids for five minutes to glue some colored tissue paper into a lively collage. Maybe we can use breakfast time to make up a story together based on one of our favorite animals. Perhaps we can grab flashlights and have a mini-living room dance party for just one song per evening. If we shift our focus from over whelmed to just one micro-moment per day, how will that change our perspective? Our kids will have that moment of connection that grounds them. We will escape from the anxious buzz in our brains by focusing entirely on something different. And, hopefully, we will all fight uncertainty by bringing a tiny bit more laughter and imagination into our daily lives. articles.text: PMS Principal Ryan Fletcher (left) and Technology Coordinator Adam Saville (right) accept the donation of LEGO Mindstorms robotics from VP Fundraising Sally Aldridge (back left) and Makers President David Ragones. Piedmont Makers donated over 30 LEGO Mindstorms Robotics sets to Piedmont Middle School in a brief ceremony at the Piedmont Middle School Makerspace on October 16. The sets were used by members of Piedmont robotic teams from 2017-2019 as part of the FIRST LEGO League program. PMS Principal Ryan Fletcher and Technology Coordinator Adam Saville were on hand to receive the donated LEGO Mindstorms. The LEGO kits are far more than toys; they include the EV3 Intelligent Brick, a compact programmable computer that can control motors and collect sensor feedback. Students can build any sort of locomotive creation from the kits, from robots, to cranes or assembly line machines. Fletcher and Saville were excited and visibly pleased to receive the LEGOs. “Both Adam and I had toured different middle schools in the area, and one component that we have continued to be interested in is exploring a robotics unit for the middle school,” said Fletcher. “With your donation, that day may be sooner rather than later, and for that I thank you,” he said nodding to Ragones and Aldridge. “It opens up a lot of flexibility for us,” he continued. “They could be used in some of our computer arts and science classes or we could include it as a unit in our makers class. There is even an opportunity with all these sets to develop a whole robotics course,” said Saville. In the last four years the Piedmont Makers robotics program has grown from one team with 10 high school students to 34 teams and 220 students from kindergarten through 12th grade. FIRST LEGO League is for students in grades 4-8. In prior years, teams have competed in local qualifier tournaments and regional championships against other regional teams. This year, the teams will compete virtually. “As the FIRST LEGO League has transitioned to a new technology platform LEGO SPIKE Prime this season, Piedmont Makers is happy to give these LEGO Mindstorms sets a future home at Piedmont Middle School,” said Ragones. “We see these as a potential fit for the 6th grade wheel or 7th-8th grade elective courses for the Fab Lab. We recognize the extraordinary work that is being done in the schools virtually and look forward to students taking advantage of this donation when they are back in the classroom.” To learn more about Piedmont robotics see: www.piedmontmakers.org or email robotics@piedmontmakers.org Photo by Joshua Posamentier 2 Piedmont Middle School students Cora Chun (left), Cassandra Colby, and Jasper Schuetz align their LEGO Mindstorms robot during a 2019 Piedmont scrimmage.
articles.title: Piedmont Makers donate robotic kits to Middle School

articles.text: In late August a group of Piedmont High School students created a club, Teens4Biden, as a way to engage students – and the entire community – in the national election November 3 to help the Biden-Harris campaign. Since then, they have been helping the campaign with phone bank work and letter writing. The organizers believe this election is incredibly important, and they want to encourage people of all ages – not just students, to help get out the vote on November 3. The club has about 30 active members, with 200 followers on Instagram. As the election nears, a Grassroots event has been planned for this Sunday, October 25. After submitting a form to the Joe Biden event portal, Teens4Biden received approval as an official campaign organization, and now is listed on the Biden-Harris website. The students will be gathering virtually on October 25 to listen to individuals, including local politicians and activists, on the importance of this election. “We want to create an environment of unity among our friends, family, neighbors and community partners,” said co-founder Audrey Edel. “We are encouraging everyone in the community to attend and support Joe Biden and Kamala Harris with us. We are in this together!” Join Teens4Biden for a virtual event this Sunday, October 25th at 5 p.m. The conferencing link to join is: h t t p s: // w w w. m o b i l i z e . u s / 2020victory/event/351889/
articles.title: Organization to host virtual rally on Sunday

articles.text: Selwyn Kumar joined the Piedmont High School faculty on September 14 as a Biology teacher. Piedmont High School started this year off without a teacher for four periods of the course, so Principal Adam Littlefield stepped up to instruct the distance learning Biology classes himself. Kumar comes to Piedmont from San Mateo High where he taught biology. Coming to a new school mid-year and teaching virtually are not new experiences for him. At San Mateo he began his teaching position in the second semester. Two months later, in March 2020 he had to adapt to distance learning even before he was fully familiar with his students, the campus and staff. “There are challenges starting during the school year. It really requires you to hit the ground running. You haven’t had the opportunity to set up curriculum or learn what you need to teach, or figure out the system of how the school works, especially when you are new. This is not the first time this has happened to me actually.” Kumar will complete his master’s degree in Education and his teaching credentials at San Jose State in March 2021. Before San Mateo High he spent a year at charter school teaching 7th grade science. Prior to that he was a substitute teacher in San Jose and Milpitas for five years. Kumar said his favorite section is science is evolution and genetics. “I find it amazing how all the diverse life we have on our planet came from one common ancestor, even if that was hundreds of millions of years ago.” He will be teaching four periods of freshman Biology in Piedmont. “It is nice to have a full staff of teachers. It allows us to have a dedicated teacher rather than having Mr. Littlefield be so stretched across multiple roles,” said science teacher John Savage. Other new faculty PHS also welcomed Dean Covalt to the science department at the start of the school year. He will teach Honors Chemistry with Savage and teach freshman Selwyn Kumar joins Piedmont High School’s faculty as a Biology teacher. Earth Science and Biology. Jorell Chavez was hired to take over the vocal music program including AP Music Theory. In the middle of the last school year, Sid Quinsaat, the acapella and AP Music Theory teacher, abandoned his teaching post and eventually quit. Retired teacher Joe Piazza eventually filled in through online teaching to help the students through the end of the school year. Other new teachers at PHS include: Ian Burns (math), Josh Ardis (social psychology) and new social studies teachers Hayley Adams and Hillary Freeman.
articles.title: PHS fills Biology, Chemistry, Acapella positions

articles.text: Users strongly encouraged to retrieve receipts from Active Net by November 8 The Recreation Department is transitioning to a new registration software, Community Pass, which will go into effect this Friday, October 23. It replaces the former registration software, Active Net. The city has primarily used Active Net for signups for about 14 years. Community Pass will cost the city less to implement and operate, and will introduce a 3-percent convenience charge for community members. The new program was chosen for its user-friendly layout and cost effectiveness. All Active Net users will be required to create an account with Community Pass to make reservations for Recreation Department activities. Active Net will only be available until November 8, after which it will be inactive. The city is strongly encouraging all families to visit their Active Net accounts and retrieve any receipts they may need for taxes and FSA accounts before November 8. All credits on Active Net accounts will be transferred to users’ Community Pass accounts Rec. Dept. bldg. after they are created. New users can create an account by signing in on register. communitypass.net and choosing “City of Piedmont, CA” as the homepage for reservations. On the welcome page, users will be able to view and pay balances, view registrations, see family member’s current registrations and edit account information. The Piedmont Recreation Department provides news and announcements that will be seen on each homepage. Residents will still need a tennis decal for court reservations. The process remains largely the same. If you purchase a new decal, the decal will be mailed to you. All players with a current decal may reserve one city court for up to two hours per day and up to one month in advance. If you already have a decal, that information will be transferred to your new Community Pass account. A facilities tab on the homepage will go live for registrations this Friday, October 23.
articles.title: Rec. Dept. starts new sign-up procedure Oct. 23

articles.text: USS Hornet Outdoor Museum - Now Open The Hornet has been open since August 1st as an openair museum. Both the Hangar Bay and flight deck are open for tours on the weekend from 10 a.m. - 5 p.m. Kids will be flying high upon seeing the 15 historic aircrafts onboard the retired aircraft carrier. Most of the helicopters, jets, and propeller planes were actually used on the Hornet. See the F8U- 1, which was flown by John Glenn in the first coast-to-coast supersonic flight. The F-4J Phantom II may be more impressive, in 1961 it set the world speed record at 1,604 mph. On-board temperature checks and masks are mandatory. Children’s Fairyland Outdoor Park - Now Open Fairyland opened its Fairy Gates October 3. To ensure safety, puppet shows, Toddler Storytimes, live performances and rides have been put on pause until getting the OK from the County Health Department. All tickets are reduced to $8. The slides are open, along with the Storybook sets. Kids can run up and roll down the Jack and Jill Hill. Gideon, Pixie, and all their other animals are ready to see the return of families. The cafe will be open for snacks. A special Halloween Jam October 28- November 1 will feature a Monster Mash parade and is sure to be a fun place to show off your costume. The park is open Wednesday to Sunday. Museum of Children’s Arts (MOCHA) Daycare and Distance Learning Assistance MOCHA has started an “Equitable Pod” program at the museum for parents that need daycare and want their kids to be in a fun environment during distance learning. Staff members will assist kids in logging into their virtual classes and answering questions. Classes consist of 10-12 kids per stable pod aged 5-12, masks and social distancing are required throughout. An hour lunch time and two break times will let kids have a chance to run around and play games outside. articles.text: The playground in Piedmont Park reopened last Friday, October 16. City-owned park playgrounds were given the green-light last Friday, October 16, by the state and county to reopen. The four city-operated playgrounds are located at Hampton Park, Piedmont Park, Dracena Park, and by Linda Beach Field and are now open to the public. The California Department of Public Health announced the reopening on September 28 and laid out extensive rules and guidance for playground visitors. Many counties in the Bay Area, including Alameda County, chose to open later than the state allowance. Piedmont announced the reopening in its COVID-19 newsletter update and stressed that the city is relying on all residents to follow the rules and use the playground safely. Parents and caregivers will need to closely monitor children to ensure the rules are followed. The city will not have monitors at playground sites. If rules are not followed, these areas may need to be closed again for noncompliance. The City staff made the decision in the past to close Linda Beach Field due to noncompliance with county health orders. The state’s health directives for playgrounds include: • Everyone over two years of age should wear a mask covering their nose and mouth. • Maintain physical distance of six feet between individuals from different households, and prevent the crowding of children. • Do not eat or drink in public playgrounds to ensure that masks are worn at all time. • Wash or sanitize hands before and after your visit. • Visit the park at different times or days to avoid crowds; limit your visit to 30 minutes when others are waiting. • Elderly residents and people with medical conditions should avoid playgrounds when others are present. Alameda County entered the less-restrictive “orange tier” of COVID health guidance on October 13, which permitted additional outdoor activities to resume. The Alameda County Health Care Services Agency will use the coming weeks to monitor the impact of students returning to school and the additional activities opened in the county to determine which, if any, additional activities may be considered for opening. “We are glad to see improving case rates and decreasing test positivity, including among our communities of color, but we caution residents that cases can rise very quickly, as we saw during the summer surge,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer. “Especially with flu season coming, if we see spikes in COVID-19 cases and a rise in hospitalizations, we will take action to limit the spread and protect public health including resuming restrictions if needed.”

Dept. starts new sign-up procedure Oct. 23 Users strongly encouraged to retrieve receipts from Active Net by November 8 By Allyson Aleksey The Recreation Department is transitioning to a new registration software, Community Pass, which will go into effect this Friday, October 23. It replaces the former registration software, Active Net. The city has primarily used Active Net for signups for about 14 years. Community Pass will cost the city less to implement and operate, and will introduce a 3-percent convenience charge for community members. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

What has remained the same, however, is my commitment to put my experience, work ethic and energy to work to represent Piedmonters for four more years. 2 – A successful committee is one that includes diverse community perspectives from those who most use our streets and sidewalks. When forming this committee, I advocated for expanding the size of the committee to increase the diversity of perspectives able to be represented in a larger group of people. For example, instead of just one student we added a second, because students, who are almost all non-drivers, spend all of their own time commuting around town by foot or on bike. They know our streets and sidewalks as well as or better than many adults do. A successful committee is one that weighs all uses of our streets and sidewalks and considers tradeoffs and potential unintended consequences when proposing changes to the current uses, configuration, signage, markings. Many of our streets are narrow; some intersections are blind and others are strangely wide-open. There is no one-size fit-all approach that will improve our streets, so careful blockby-block recommendations will have to be developed. A successful committee is one that incorporates input from as many residents and users as possible. The meetings are always open to everyone. And yet not everyone is available to attend meetings in person, even virtual ones. So alternate means should be available to include as many voices as possible. In the end, the goal will be to have a plan for potential city improvements that will make our streets safer for bicyclists and pedestrians, wheelchairs and strollers, so they can get around town alongside autos and buses. articles.text: In advance of the November 3 municipal election, City Council candidates were asked two questions: 1) How has your experience been running for office? 2) What are the benefits to the city if the Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee proves to be successful? articles.text: Measure UU is the result of thoughtful preparation and widespread community effort over many years. In 2016, the City Council formed an Aquatics Master Plan Steering Committee and hired pool experts Counsilman-Hunsaker, and LEED certified architects, Harley Ellis Devereaux (HED), to work with City staff and over 100 members of the community to develop a conceptual plan for the inevitable replacement of the Piedmont Pool. The conceptual plan that arose from that public process is reflected in Measure UU. There are over 350 pages of review, study, and discussion, including a 2018 report on the pool’s deteriorating condition, all of which is available to the public on the City’s website. The fact is that outdoor concrete pools do not last forever, and the 56-year-old Piedmont Pool has reached the end of its viability. There are no more lowcost fixes or patches that can save the disintegrating decks, fix the massive leaks, or address the chronically failing mechanical equipment. There is no Plan B. articles.text: Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (“PRFO”) mission statement reads: ”PRFO works collaboratively with the City of Piedmont to identify, advocate for, and bring private financial support to assist in the funding of projects that invest in healthy spaces within the city.” The tagline for PRFO is “Working Together so we can Play Together.” Never have these words been more relevant than in the City’s commitment to rebuild the Piedmont Pool complex through the passage of Measure UU. The Piedmont Pool is an iconic part of the community where generations of Piedmont residents have enjoyed the outdoors. Our one and only public pool is also an essential facility providing a safe and healthy place for families to enjoy aquatics. In addition to the community usage, it also provides Piedmont students the opportunity to compete in swimming and water polo which promotes teamwork, commitment, discipline, and drive. All important qualities as they embark on their life journeys. In support of its mission, PRFO has partnered with the City in the renovation of Hampton Park and the conversion of the City’s Vista tennis courts into the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Community enthusiasm and support have made these projects a reality through private financial contributions of over $1,300,000. The catalyst for the success of these fundraising initiatives has been the City’s willingness to take the lead and commit funding first. Then PRFO, in partnership with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (“PBF”) and other community groups, has been able to rally private donations to support the success of these improvements. The boards of PRFO and PBF have both endorsed Measure UU. Should Measure UU pass, and if asked by the City, PRFO would be willing and ready to rally community financial support for the Piedmont Pool. But first things first, the voters of Piedmont need to decide if they want the City to rebuild a pool for the next 50 years. For the sake of the health of our community, I hope the answer is yes. Steve Collins is President of Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization

articles.text: Below are answers to frequently asked questions regarding Measure UU, which, if approved, would authorize the issuance of general obligation bonds to replace the Piedmont Community Pool. 1. The City proposes to issue $19.5 Million in bonds. What is the actual expected borrowing interest rate assuming the bond passes this year? Municipal bonds can be issued in stages as the funds are needed, and the applicable interest rate is determined at the time the bonds are issued. As a frame of reference, the interest rate as of September 16, 2020 is 2.8%. 2. What is the City’s current total outstanding general obligation debt? The City currently has no outstanding general obligation debt. 3. What is the term of the bond repayment? Measure UU provides that the term of the bond repayment is 30 years with a fixed interest rate. 4. How long will the tax be imposed on properties, and will the amount of the tax ever decrease? Measure UU, if adopted, would impose a tax on properties for 30 years. In the event our property tax roll increases at 3.5% per year (10 year average is ~4.5%), the tax rate per $1,000 of assessed value will drop from $0.26 (if all bonds are issued) to approximately $0.10 in thirty years. The total tax assessed would still be the same, but redistributed based on the individual property assessment. 5. How can a property owner ascertain the assessed value of property? Each year, the Alameda County Assessor’s Office notifies all property owners of the property’s annual assessed value. This number can also be found on a property owner’s property tax bill. Residents can ascertain the assessed value of their home on the Alameda County Assessor’s web site. 6. How does Measure UU impact the City’s General Fund? Measure UU does not have an impact on the City’s General Fund. 7. What is the proposed concept for replacing the existing pool? In the event Measure UU is adopted, the exact design of the pool facility will be finalized through a public process. The current proposed concept to replace the existing pool is the establishment of two pools: (1) a warmer, shallower recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation, and (2) a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. Jen4Piedmont.com Paid for by Jen Cavenaugh for City Council 2020 FPPC #PENDING PRFO voices its support of Pool Bond, Measure UU By Steve Collins Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (“PRFO”) mission statement reads: ”PRFO works collaboratively with the City of Piedmont to identify, advocate for, and bring private financial support to assist in the funding of projects that invest in healthy spaces within the city.” The tagline for PRFO is “Working Together so we can Play Together.” Never have these words been more relevant than in the City’s commitment to rebuild the Piedmont Pool complex through the passage of Measure UU. The Piedmont Pool is an iconic part of the community where generations of Piedmont residents have enjoyed the outdoors. Our one and only public pool is also an essential facility providing a safe and healthy place for families to enjoy aquatics. In addition to the community usage, it also provides Piedmont students the opportunity to compete in swimming and water polo which promotes teamwork, commitment, discipline, and drive. All important qualities as they embark on their life journeys. In support of its mission, PRFO has partnered with the City in the renovation of Hampton Park and the conversion of the City’s Vista tennis courts into the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Community enthusiasm and support have made these projects a reality through private financial contributions of over $1,300,000. The catalyst for the success of these fundraising initiatives has been the City’s willingness to take the lead and commit funding first. Then PRFO, in partnership with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (“PBF”) and other community groups, has been able to rally private donations to support the success of these improvements. The boards of PRFO and PBF have both endorsed Measure UU. Should Measure UU pass, and if asked by the City, PRFO would be willing and ready to rally community financial support for the Piedmont Pool. But first things first, the voters of Piedmont need to decide if they want the City to rebuild a pool for the next 50 years. For the sake of the health of our community, I hope the answer is yes. Steve Collins is President of Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization City of Piedmont’s F.A.Q. on Pool Bond Below are answers to frequently asked questions regarding Measure UU, which, if approved, would authorize the issuance of general obligation bonds to replace the Piedmont Community Pool. 1. The City proposes to issue $19.5 Million in bonds. What is the actual expected borrowing interest rate assuming the bond passes this year? Municipal bonds can be issued in stages as the funds are needed, and the applicable interest rate is determined at the time the bonds are issued. As a frame of reference, the interest rate as of September 16, 2020 is 2.8%. 2. What is the City’s current total outstanding general obligation debt? The City currently has no outstanding general obligation debt. 3. What is the term of the bond repayment? Measure UU provides that the term of the bond repayment is 30 years with a fixed interest rate. 4. How long will the tax be imposed on properties, and will the amount of the tax ever decrease? Measure UU, if adopted, would impose a tax on properties for 30 years. In the event our property tax roll increases at 3.5% per year (10 year average is ~4.5%), the tax rate per $1,000 of assessed value will drop from $0.26 (if all bonds are issued) to approximately $0.10 in thirty years. The total tax assessed would still be the same, but redistributed based on the individual property assessment. 5. How can a property owner ascertain the assessed value of property? Each year, the Alameda County Assessor’s Office notifies all property owners of the property’s annual assessed value. This number can also be found on a property owner’s property tax bill. Residents can ascertain the assessed value of their home on the Alameda County Assessor’s web site. 6. How does Measure UU impact the City’s General Fund? Measure UU does not have an impact on the City’s General Fund. 7. What is the proposed concept for replacing the existing pool? In the event Measure UU is adopted, the exact design of the pool facility will be finalized through a public process. The current proposed concept to replace the existing pool is the establishment of two pools: (1) a warmer, shallower recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation, and (2) a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. Each pool would be larger See Measure UU FAQ on page 28

articles.text: Members of the girl’s water polo team voiced their support of Measure UU, including PHS senior Grace Davies in an open letter. Measure UU is undoubtedly the marquee items on Piedmont’s November ballot. One flip through the Post the last month makes you aware. For athletes at Piedmont High, the measure means a legitimate future worth planning for and looking forward to. UU has undertaken a giant community effort, which had a student-led rally on Wednesday, October 14 at the corner of Highland and Oakland Avenue. Around 25 current and former student-athletes from Piedmont High attended the rally, organized by Piedmont Swim Team captain and PHS student Noah Kwong. Students and alumni are also taking a big role in social media outreach, in addition to helping manage the Measure UU campaign website: https://www.communitypoolforpiedmont.com/ Current Piedmont High senior Grace Davies wrote an official letter to help urge eligible voters in town to supply their “Yes” on the ballot, noting her experience on the water polo team and her time working as a lifeguard. “Being a part of the pool community through water polo opened my eyes to another great skill and opportunity for me — lifeguarding and teaching swim lessons. The pool provided the training and certifications for me to have a flexible work experience that was also very fulfilling. I can’t imagine a more convenient job for a PHS student — I could walk to work after school and schedule my hours around my other activities. Not only did I earn a paycheck, but I had an impact on others and got to work with a great community of staff at the pool,” she wrote. “Please remember the students when you consider your vote — and how much we all benefit from this project. We need to continue the tradition of a community pool and swimming program in Piedmont. Please vote YES on Measure UU for the future of swimming in Piedmont,” Davies continued. For mer Piedmont High All-American water polo athlete Henry Saunders (Class of 2019), now at USC, talked about the need of a new pool in town. Saunders set school records in the Piedmont pool and is now a member of perennial powerhouse USC. He has described the Piedmont Pool the “worst” he’s ever played in, and a place that precluded having a home-crowd atmosphere similar to other sports. “As a 2015-2019 PHS Water Polo and Swim athlete, I am a strong supporter of Yes on UU. I am very proud to have been raised in Piedmont, attended Piedmont schools K-12 and swam my first strokes in the Piedmont pool with my Grandfather,” wrote Saunders. “While I have fond memories of the Piedmont Pool, it is not the competitive pool Piedmont swimmers and water polo players deserve. I am very fortunate to have played regional and national water polo tournaments over the past 10 years and truthfully, the Piedmont Pool is unfortunately the worst pool I have competed in,” he continued. Saunders reiterated the sentiments of his former Piedmont High head coach John Savage, that the water polo program will not survive without the funding toward a new pool. “The Piedmont water polo program has great coaches and is growing as well, but it may die altogether if the Piedmont pool isn’t rebuilt. Every other city in Alameda County provides a pool for its students. Piedmont students deserve the same,” he wrote. For more information, visit the campaign site of Measure UU: https://www.communitypoolforpiedmont.com/. Former Piedmont High All-American Henry Saunders, now at USC, is in strong support of Measure UU which would create a new pool in town.

articles.text: East Bay Regional Parks re-opened their hill-based parks on Friday, October 16, after high winds threatened the area with possible extreme fire activity. Of parks re-opened, all are within miles of Piedmont: Anthony Chabot Regional Park, Claremont Canyon Regional Preserve, Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve, Kennedy Grove Regional Recreation Area, Leona Canyon Open Space Regional Preserve, Reinhardt Redwood Regional Park, Roberts Regional Recreation Area, Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve, Tilden Regional Park, Wildcat Canyon Regional Park Figuring out which parks to visit during fire season can be a confusing task. Aside from checking our weekly outdoors information in this section of the Piedmont Post, East Bay Regional lists the status of all parks at: ebparks.org. Although the SCU Complez Fire was contained in 44 days as of October 1, parks within the East Bay Regional Park District remain closed, including Castle Rock of the Diablo Foothills, the Morgan Territory Regional Preserve of Contra Costa County, Alameda Count y’s Sunol Regional Wilderness near Sunol and Hayward and the Ohlone Wilderness near Fremont. Earlier this month the park district announced that dogs are again, permitted to be off-leash in designated areas. “We thank dog owners for their understanding during COVID-19 and their cooperation with the temporary leash restrictions,” said East Bay Regional’s general manager Robert Doyle. “The restrictions have helped keep parks and trails open and safe. Regional Parks, now more than ever, play an important role in maintaining mental health and providing places where people and their pets can exercise in a safe, socially distant manner.” This does not mean that dogs are totally allowed to roam free, EBRP reminds. Dogs must still be leashed in parking lots, trailheads, and paved bike paths. “The return of normal dog rules is a reminder that dog owners need to be responsible and share the parks with others,” added Doyle. “Dog owners need to bag and bin their dog’s poop, leash their dogs in designated areas, including parking lots, trailheads, and paved trails, and keep their dogs on-leash around cattle and horses. Cattle play an important role in reducing vegetation and fire risks.” A closed East Bay Regional Park. Staff Photo
articles.title: East Bay Parks reopen after brief closure

articles.text: It’s never too early to start examining the United States Men’s National Team, which should have no problem qualifying for the 2022 World Cup, right? Well, it’s not that simple. Not qualifying for the 2018 World Cup was a huge disappointment; and with the squad not appearing again until 2021, the U.S, seemingly has a much tighter time frame to get into form and determine its best 23 players. The United States isn’t scheduled for matches until the 2022 World Cup Qualifiers, which will take place between June 2021 and March 2022. The World Cup qualifier overlaps with the 2021 CONCACAF Gold Cup in July 2021. U.S. manager Gregg Berhalter announced the team would focus on arranging two European friendlies in November and some domestic matches this fall, however nothing is set at this point. Luckily for the U.S., the team automatically qualified for the final round of the World Cup qualifier along with Mexico, Costa Rica, Jamaica, and Honduras based on FIFA world rankings. The final round of World Cup Qualifiers will be an eightteam, single group round-robin of matches, with the top three teams automatically qualifying for the World Cup. A fourth CONCACAF team will qualify for FIFA’s Inter-Confederation playoffs to determine the last two teams in the World Cup. Inter-Confederation matches will be made up of one team from CONCACAF (North America), CONMEBOL (South America), OFC (Oceanic), and AFC (Asian). As for the U.S. roster, this writer wastes no time calling their future 2022 World Cup roster the start of its Golden Generation of players. It makes the possibility of not qualifying a terrifying thought. The U.S. will have nearly an entire roster of players under age 30, many of who play overseas in England, Germany, Spain, and France. Though matches will be limited for the next year, here is our look at the possible 23-man roster for the 2022 World Cup. CDM Kellyn Acosta (Colorado Rapids), CDM Jackson Yueill (San Jose Earthquakes), CAM Brenden Aaronson (RB Salzburg), CAM Richie Ledezma (PSV Einhoven) Weston McKennie, Tyler Adams, and Giovanni Reyna are three headliners overseas in Italy’s Serie A and Germany’s Bundesliga – each gaining valuable Champions League experience. Reyna is only 17-years old and could be a star in the making. Behind them it gets a little tougher and is visibly the weakest area of the roster. In need of defensive mids, Kellyn Acosta of the Colorado Rapids and Jackson Yueill from the San Jose Earthquakes could certainly be of use. But, attacking options with experience are bleak. Brenden Aaronson, 19, is joining Bundesliga’s RB Salzburg after making 45 appearances with the Philadelphia Union. Richie Ledezma, 20, plays for the Netherlands’ PSV Einhoven. However, Aaronson has one USMNT appearance and Ledezma has only three for the U23 team. The lack of experience on the backend could result in former captain Michael Bradley appearing as a veteran backup. Fellow veteran CM Paul Arriola also seems logical but also less than ideal. Defense: LB Sergino Dest (Barcelona), LB Antonee Robinson (Fulham), RB DeAndre Yedlin (Newcastle), RB Reggie Cannon (FC Dallas), CB John Brooks (Wolfsburg), CB Matt Miazga (Reading), CB Miles Robinson (Atlanta Utd) Sergino Dest, the 19-year old phenom made headlines when signing with Barcelona. He’s a major upgrade at wingback and is likely to suit up on the left. DeAndre Yedlin is among the Forward: LW Christian Pulisic (Chelsea), RW Tim Weah (Lille), FW Tyler Boyd (Beksitas), FW Jordan Morris (Seattle Sounders), ST Josh Sargent (Wolfsburg), ST Jozy Altidore (Toronto FC) The United States will have lots of speed and attacking options in 2022 like Tim Weah, who must prove he can stay healthy with Lille in France, and Chelsea’s Christian Pulisic, who will be the talisman and could line up at wing or central attacking midfield. The interesting subject of this group will be Jozy Altidore, who at age 32 should be the veteran leader in the locker room. But he’s sure to face competition for playing time from Josh Sargent and Jordan Morris – both younger and faster options. Another name to keep an eye on is Wolfsburg’s 19-year old Ulysses Llanez. However, it’s hard to see Llanez pushing for a spot with limited time due to COVID. Midfield: CM Weston McKennie (Juventus), CDM Tyler Adams (RB Leipzig), CAM Giovanni Reyna (Dortmund), Men’s soccer team manager Gregg Berhalter. most experienced and should start on the opposite side if he’s healthy. The United States is deepest at center back, meaning some talented players could miss out. John Brooks is the unquestioned captain and a regular starter for Germany’s Wolfsburg. Next to him could be Matt Miazga, who has been playing well in England, while Miles Robinson is considered a surging talent in the MLS. If Miazga and Robinson crack the 23-man roster, that means they will have unseated veterans Aaron Long and Tim Ream. Given that Ream can double as a left back and center back, he could be someone to keep an eye on despite being 35 when the World Cup starts. Goalkeeper: Zac Steffen (Fortuna Dusseldorf), Ethan Horvath (Club Brugge), Brad Guzan (Atlanta Utd) Zac Steffen, on loan to Dusseldorf from Manchester City, is the unquestioned leader at keeper. Behind him is a mere formality; Ethan Horvath plays for Club Brugge and is gaining Champions League experience this season. Brad Guzan could be a farfetched thought at 38-years old in 2022, but opting for experience could prove useful from a leadership standpoint. American soccer fans should get to know 17-year Gio Reyna of Borussia.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of LA Times 49ers cornerback Jason Verrett snatched a critical interception in a 24-16 win over the Rams last Sunday, October 18. Here we go again. The 49ers have yet again proven my predictions wrong after upsetting the Los Angeles Rams 24-16 last Sunday. Although San Francisco didn’t get any sacks, they rushed Rams QB Jared Goff into completing just 19 of 38 passes for 198 yards, two touchdowns, but a critical interception for Jason Verrett in the end zone. San Francisco QB Jimmy Garoppolo had a bounce-back game with three touchdowns and 268 yards passing. And when looking ahead to Week 7’s matchup with the Patriots, he’ll need to be as efficient. New England has among the best pass defenses in the league, but they are vulnerable without many weapons aside from quarterback Cam Newton. In the end, if Garoppolo and 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan are in sync, San Francisco could walk away with a big victory. If it becomes a defensive battle, the edge has to go toward the Patriots and its coach Bill Belichick. Raiders update The Raiders return from their bye week with a visit from Tom Brady and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Jon Gruden and Las Vegas have proven to do well in critical games this season, but this writer expects it will be a tough defensive battle. Tampa Bay has the 2nd best run defense in the league, meaning if Vegas can’t get Josh Jacobs going and become one-dimensional, it’s going to get tough. If the Raiders come out with a win, it will be becauseQB Derrick Carr is efficient with his throws and maybe lands a bomb or two with rookie WR Henry Ruggs. Premier League review Crossing the pond to England, Premier League returned from the international break for its fifth of 38 match days. Everton and Liverpool’s Merseyside Derby had the game of the week in a 2-2 draw, meaning Everton continues undefeated at 4-1-0 and first place of the league table. The match was highlighted in what would’ve been the game winning goal by Liverpool’s Jordan Henderson after VAR ruled Sadio Mane offside, while Liverpool defender Virgil Van Dijk sustained a season-ending knee injury. Aston Villa continues its unexpected winstreak to four games after defeating Leicester 1-0 when recent acquisition Ross Barkley scored the game-winner in the first of five minutes of stoppage time. The Lions are 4-0-0 and in second, a point behind the Toffees. Looking ahead to Matchday 6, some big games are happening with large implications on the table. Aston Villa square off with recently promoted Leeds on Friday, and Leeds are surprisingly listed as the favorite. Villa will surely face an uphill battle each week and, at some point, will dip down the table. But saying it will start against Leeds could be a bit of a stretch. Manchester United is currently in 15th of 20 with six points at 2-0-2, they’ll play Chelsea on Saturday—who are in 8th at 2-2-1. United are coming off a big 2-1 victory over PSG in their Champions League meeting on Tuesday, while Chelsea drew 3-3 with Southampton and are allowing a lot of goals. This could be time for the Reds to pounce. Everton and Southampton meet on Sunday, this writer could see a draw with Southampton’s Danny Ings in a great run of form. Arsenal and Leceister are another key match with the Gunners in fifth (3-0-2) and Foxes in fourth (3-0-2). Photo courtesy of The Guardian Aston Villa is still undefeated at 4-0-0. Can they continue their impressive run against Leeds this week?
articles.title: 49ers upset Rams; Premier League preview

articles.text: It’s no surprise Piedmont kids are the number one supporters and advocates to rebuild the failing Piedmont Pool. It is children who will most benefit from a new facility. The kids will undoubtedly be harmed if Piedmont voters don’t pass Measure UU on November 3. Even though over 90% of them can’t vote, hundreds of Piedmont kids of all ages are walking the streets, writing letters, waving signs, posting on social media, creating a video and website, and making calls – all urging adult voters in town to think about the future of young people without any pool in the city. Nearly all Piedmont children use the pool for swim lessons, recreation, summer camps, PE, and athletics. If Piedmont doesn’t rebuild its pool, it will be the only city in Alameda County that doesn’t provide a pool for its families and students. “To many adults in town, Measure UU is just another line on their ballot. Some could even flip a coin on rebuilding the pool. But to Piedmont youth, the outcome of Measure UU will completely change our lives,” said Noah Kwong, captain of the Piedmont Swim Team. On Wednesday, October 14 during the afternoon rush hour, Piedmont youth ranging from first grade to recent Piedmont High School graduates rallied together at the intersection of Highland and Oakland Avenues, waving signs and placards in support of Measure UU. Supporters honked, gave the thumbs up, and cheered on the student athletes. In addition to the omnipresent blue Yes on UU signs, kids created homemade signs with words straight from their heart, including: “I don’t want to have to carpool to Orinda or Alameda just to swim!” “We have courts and fields. Where’s our Pool ” “I’m a basketball player, not a swimmer, but I’m out here in Sonja ten Grotenhuis (left), Madeline Payne, and Daniela Acevedo-Schiesel. solidarity with my fellow PHS athletes. A pool is just as important to our athletic program as a gym,” said Luke Harris, a recent recruit to play basketball at Carleton College. “Water Polo has changed our lives and those of our teammates. Without a pool in Piedmont, there are many who will have to quit the sport because of the high cost to rent space in another community’s pool, and the time it will take to commute to practice,” said Ella Wright and Spencer Stein, PHS water polo players. For the next few weeks, youth across town will continue to juggle online class work and campaign for Measure UU. For many, the campaign for a Piedmont Community Pool has been their first foray into politics. “As a swimmer, my heart is in this fight, and as a student, it’s been interesting to learn the political side of things,” said Gwenyth Jones, a PHS swimmer. “There’s so much at stake in this election from the top of the ballot down to Measure UU.” Piedmont’s youth will be watching the election returns on November 3rd, just like the adults in town. Piedmont Middle School seventh grader, Tai March-Cunningham summed up the kids’ perspective. “Adults had a pool when they were growing up. Why wouldn’t they vote for us to have one, too?” Water polo players Ella Wright (left), Hannah Mooney, Grace Davies, and Gwenyth Jones. Deniz Radzik (left), Kate Aubrecht, Josie Oesterer, Miles the dog, and Noah Kwong attend a rally in favor of a bond to build a new pool in Piedmont. Piedmont Swim team members encourage motorists to support Measure UU. Pictured are Farris Saffouri (left), Charlie White, Aaron Wu, Simon Lins, Brian Wu and Ryan Stokes.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse has announced its revised 2020–21 season, presented in a series of acts. Each act will be comprised of three shows for a total of nine productions. Act I will put talent back onstage again for a series of on-demand video streams. Act I: Taking the Leap will run from October 24 through December 31. It will consist of three video on-demand offerings from some of the Bay Area’s greatest artists as well as playwrights from across the globe. All three productions will be available for on-demand video streaming. The first work in Taking the Leap features a play by Yasmina Reza, directed by Bill English and starring Bobak Cyrus Bakhtiari, Johnny Moreno, and Jomar Tagatac. The play, entitled Art, explores how an upcoming election creates division between opposing camps. Although it is a comedy, it explores and addresses the complex layers of friendship. The show will stream from October 24 to November 7. The Jewelry Box, written and performed by Brian Copeland, will follow in Act I. In this story, a prequel to Copeland’s hit solo show Not a Genuine Black Man, a young Brian heads to the mean streets of Oakland to buy his mother a Christmas gift. When he finds the perfect present – a jewelry box in the White Front store – six-year-old Brian sets out to earn the required $11.97 by Christmas Eve. The Jewelry Box will stream from November 28 to December 25. The entrance to San Francisco Playhouse at 450 Post Street. The final work scheduled for the holidays is From Blues to Broadway. It was created in collaboration with and performed by John Paul Gonzalez, Cate Hayman, Rodney Earl Jackson, Jr., and Katrina Lauren McGraw, with music direction by Dave Dobrusky. In this piece, Dobrusky directs a who’s who of San Francisco musical talent. Hayman, McGraw, Jackson, and Gonzalez will perform a medley of holiday songs. The piece will stream from December 12 through December 31. Act II and Act III will be announced in the near future. Subscribe to Act I plays at https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ sfph/2020-2021-season/.
articles.title: SF Playhouse season to begin October 24

articles.text: Violinist Lisa Lee will appear in a concert with Musaics of the Bay. Musaics of the Bay will present a Shubert concert performed by five Bay Area musicians on November 8. Schubert’s Cello Quintet in C Major, D. 956 will be performed by violinists Lisa Lee (one fifth of The Lee Trio) and Francisco Fullana, Jonathan Vinocour on viola, and cellists Peter Myers and Tanya Tomkins. Lee is a Fulbright Scholar and top prizewinner in the Tadeusz Wronski International Violin Competition, Pacific Symphony Orchestra Young Artists, and San Francisco Symphony Concerto competitions. She and her two sisters perform internationally as The Lee Trio and have appeared at the Piedmont Center of the Arts. She has been on the faculty at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music since 2017. Fullana, winner of the 2018 Avery Fisher Career Grant, is a native of Mallorca in Spain. He has soloed with the City of Birmingham, Vancouver, Pacific, and Madrid Symphonies as well as the Saint Paul Chamber Orchestra and the Spanish Radio Television Orchestra. Vinocour was appointed Principal Viola of the San Francisco Symphony in 2009. He previously was Principal Viola of the Saint Louis Symphony and Guest Principal of the Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig. Myers has served as an assistant Principal Cellist of the San Francisco Opera since 2017 and is internationally known as a chamber musician. Cellist Tomkins is renowned in particular for her interpretation of the Bach Cello Suites, which she has performed many times at venues including New York’s Le Poisson Rouge and the Seattle Early Music Guild. The virtual premiere on Sunday, November 8, includes a pre-concert Zoom discussion and post-performance artist reception. There is a $3 reservation fee, and a suggested $10 donation. The pre-concert discussion will begin at 3:45 p.m., and the performance will commence at 4 p.m. To reserve your spot, visit h t t p s: // w w w. m u s a i c s .o r g / virtualconcerts. articles.text: Oakland Symphony, as part of its “rePAST” archival concert streaming series, is celebrating Indigenous Peoples’ Day with a performance of John Christopher Wineglass’ Big Sur: The Night Sun. “The natural beauty of Big Sur is sacred to many. This feeling of sanctity was shared by Wineglass, who formed many of the themes of his tone poem Big Sur: The Night Sun while in residence on the grounds of the Glen Deven Ranch and other areas such as Pfeiffer Beach,” Music Director Michael Morgan explained. “The beautiful impressions and warm enlightenments that affected him while on the retreat become the root and soul of this magnificent work.” The performance features Emiliano Campobello on native flute, Marcie Chapa and Jayson Fann as world percussionists, and Kanyon Sayers-Roods, Native-American singer from the Costanoan Ohlone and Chumash Tribes. “This mesmerizing work features the haunting voice of Kanyon Sayers-Roods, her art is a sincere expression of her native heritage,” Morgan said. The piece was originally performed by the symphony at the Paramount Theatre on February 24, 2017, and is available online at https://www.oaklandsymphony. org/repast/.
articles.title: Oakland Symphony celebrates Indigenous Peoples’ Day

articles.text: Barns in Ferndale Local artist Michael Stehr will present his latest collection of paintings at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from October 30 through November 8. The exhibition, entitled “The Sky’s the Limit,” will focus on skies in landscape and cityscape work, and will show how the nature of sky affects mood and atmosphere. The exhibit marks the first opportunity to show his paintings since the pandemic limited public events seven months ago. Because his series of art lectures at the Center was interrupted due to COVID, he has had several free virtual art history lectures to stay connected with his audience. The Zoom lectures were very well attended, confirming Piedmont’s desire to connect to the arts during the pandemic. On Friday, October 30, Stehr will host a virtual opening of the art exhibit via Zoom starting at 6 p.m. During the presentation he will discuss details of his construction of skies: how the sky is rendered, the effect of using certain values, the forms of cloud composition, and the utilization of certain color harmonies as a way of achieving a particular feel for the painting. Stehr will also preview 36 new paintings, along with other previously exhibited work, to complete the robust exhibit. Reservations are required to visit the gallery in person. The exhibit will be open on Saturday and Sunday, October 31 and November 1, and Saturday and Sunday, November 7 and 8, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Visits will be at 30-minute intervals. A link to the reservation sign-up sheet can be found on the PCA website (www. piedmontcenterforthearts.org) or by visiting michaelstehr.com. Coastline at Normandy
articles.title: For artist Michael Stehr, the Sky’s The Limit

Oakland Symphony celebrates Indigenous Peoples’ Day By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Symphony, as part of its “rePAST” archival concert streaming series, is celebrating Indigenous Peoples’ Day with a performance of John Christopher Wineglass’ Big Sur: The Night Sun. “The natural beauty of Big Sur is sacred to many. This feeling of sanctity was shared by Wineglass, who formed many of the themes of his tone poem Big Sur: The Night Sun while in residence on the grounds of the Glen Deven Ranch and other areas such as Pfeiffer Beach,” Music Director Michael Morgan explained. “The beautiful impressions and warm enlightenments that affected him while on the retreat become the root and soul of this magnificent work.” The performance features Emiliano Campobello on native flute, Marcie Chapa and Jayson Fann as world percussionists, and Kanyon Sayers-Roods, Native-American singer from the Costanoan Ohlone and Chumash Tribes. “This mesmerizing work features the haunting voice of Kanyon Sayers-Roods, her art is a sincere expression of her native heritage,” Morgan said. For artist Michael Stehr, the Sky’s The Limit Barns in Ferndale Local artist Michael Stehr will present his latest collection of paintings at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from October 30 through November 8. The exhibition, entitled “The Sky’s the Limit,” will focus on skies in landscape and cityscape work, and will show how the nature of sky affects mood and atmosphere. The exhibit marks the first opportunity to show his paintings since the pandemic limited public events seven months ago. Because his series of art lectures at the Center was interrupted due to COVID, he has had several free virtual art history lectures to stay connected with his audience.
