articles.text: American pop and jazz singer Frank Sinatra. The name Frank Sinatra conjures up deep feelings. Some say that he was the greatest pop singer of them all. Others assert, with equal fervor, that his fame was ill-deserved. No matter which side you were on, everyone had to agree that Sinatra had a distinctive style. I’m not talking about the way he dressed...which was the epitome of high fashion. I am speaking of the way he sang. No one sang a song like Sinatra. He was so stylish that he remained popular long after his voice had deserted him. It might shock you to know that he did not invent his style of singing. Critics, in their effort to analyze Sinatra’s success, claim that he patterned his singing after crooners like Bing Crosby. But if you really listen to Sinatra’s singing technique, perhaps you will understand and agree with me that Sinatra was actually inspired by the popular operatic baritone John Charles Thomas. Sinatra famously sang on consonants, a technique he got from John Charles Thomas. Sometimes Sinatra sang a combination of talking through a song and actually singing. He got this technique from John Charles Thomas. Sinatra caressed a phrase like no one else – also something he learned from John Charles Thomas. So, dear readers, listen to some recordings of Sinatra in his prime. And then listen to some of the songs that made John Charles Thomas so popular. First listen to some of his serious operatic arias. Then listen to his wisecracking rendition of Largo al factotum by Rossini. Follow this with a western song such as “Home on the Range,” and finally listen to his rendition of a kid’s song, “The Green Eyed Dragon with the 13 Tails.” It’s hard to believe that two singers who were 180° apart in type of music being sung could approach a song the same way. But they did. And each one was a phenomenal success. Now we will take a quick segue from vintage Sinatra to vintage wines. A friend who is in the communications business sent me a short piece on wine. Back in prehistoric times, our predecessors discovered that wine and other alcoholic beverages were actually safer to drink than water. Wine was quite easy to make. Grape juice and sugar-consuming yeast transform into wine. Actually, I think that the grapes come with their own yeast. Our predecessors tried different types of grapes and different types of yeast. And that’s where the arguments and the fun began. It was red versus white, dry versus sweet, fresh wine versus aged. Let’s not forget vintage versus vintage and finally the presentation. There is evidence of fermented drinks in ancient China around 7000 BC. Around 6000 BC wine was made in Georgia and then more recently in Sicily in 4000 BC. The Spanish tried to introduce wine in California. Success came much later. We put our trust in wine connoisseurs. These experts take themselves seriously. Once, while on a concert tour in Italy, I was invited to a prize-winning winery near Florence. We went to the tasting room and the famous vintner regaled us with his expertise. All the appropriate vocabulary was used while he swirled his wine around in an elegant glass. I didn’t know if I should take the man seriously, but the famous vintner knew exactly what he was doing. With a twinkle in his eye, he concluded his discourse on winemaking by saying, “It’s all <*<>\?!” And with that, he gave us a few bottles of his famous wine and sent us on our way. American operatic baritone John Charles Thomas.
articles.title: Vintage Frank Sinatra and vintage wines

articles.text: The University of California, Berkeley Botanical Garden will host a Zoom program exploring the many species of butterflies that have taken residence in the gardens. Join the garden’s resident propagator Sal Levinson and garden volunteer Sarab Seth for an illustrated slideshow of butterflies found among the flowers this time of year. Sal Levinson commonly seen in the gardens are Cabbage White, West Coast Lady, Painted Lady, Common Buckeye, Fiery Skipper, California Ringlet, and Red Admiral. This Zoom event is suitable for all ages and includes live viewings of caterpillars. It will take place this Sunday, October 25, from 11 a.m. to 12 p.m. The event is free and open to the public. To register online, visit https://41780.blackbaudhosting. com/41780/Zoom-Program-Butterf lies-of-the-UC-BotanicalGarden-25Oct2020.

articles.text: A scene from JoJo Rabbit. Moview review by Chris Honoré The Oscar nominated film JoJo Rabbit is a high risk, high gain satire, using humor, irony and ridicule to comment on the Nazi regime during a period when Germany and Austria were fully committed to a pathological leader, millions enthusiastically raising their arms in euphoric, sieg heil approbation. So the question begged is whether it’s possible to use satire effectively when telling a story about a regime that is defined as evil. How to bring to bear even a hint of humor or exaggeration or ridicule while examining what is profoundly grim and awful? But that is what JoJo Rabbit attempts to do, choosing as its narrative vehicle a 10-year-old boy, JoJo Betzler (Roman Griffin Davis), a wide-eyed, newbie Nazi, dressed in a Hitler Youth uniform, ready to die for der Fuhrer, who also happens to be his imaginary friend. The mustachioed, strutting companion is always nearby (portrayed by writer/director Taiki Waititi), reminding JoJo that a good Nazi is a loyal Nazi, occasionally asking for a seig heil, just to keep in practice. What JoJo Rabbit serves up is a comical exaggeration with uniform-clad caricatures created to elicit a laugh, their strutting reminiscent of Charlie Chaplin’s slapstick performance in The Great Dictator. Actually, given the prism through which JoJo views his world, it’s evident that he is poorly equipped to even begin to critically evaluate the horror that surrounds him. His indoctrination has been complete, and the walls of his room are covered in fanboy Nazi propaganda. So, when JoJo discovers that his mother, Rosie (Scarlett Johansson), has been hiding a young Jewish girl, Elsa (Thomasin McKenzie), in an attic hideaway, he is instantly conflicted. He feels he should report this betrayal, reinforced vociferously by his Fuhrer; however, to do so would implicate his mother. As well, it is clear that this young boy, who simply wants to join a club of his peers and have an adventure, is completely unaware of the horror visited on the Jewish people by his swastika-wearing compatriots. His experience and understanding is far too limited. And yet, curious, taken with her, he sets out to know Elsa better, hoping to comprehend what being Jewish means. He writes her letters in the voice of her boyfriend, now missing. He asks about stereotypes, absent any understanding of the consequences of such prejudices and their entrenched racism. And so as Waititi uses satire; in the aggregate is seems no more then cute but pointless. JoJo’s point of view is framed by his naiveté and childlike innocence and so he is insulated from the awful truths that surround him. In one scene when he is passing through the town square he sees condemned Germans who have been hanged, their still bodies, hands bound, turning slowly in a light wind. He, of course, is incapable of making a connection between what he sees before him and his love of Nazism or the red swastika armband he proudly wears, or the meaning of his imaginary friend. For JoJo this hideous image of the hanged, filled with a remorseless finality, is devoid of implication and to connect what he sees to all that he dearly wants to be is a bridge too far. He’s just a kid. And therein is the flaw in the film. Its use of satire has no edge, no restrained rage, limited even in its final scenes by JoJo’s obliviousness. Humor, sarcasm, ridicule or exaggeration cannot save this story from a darkness that is beyond comprehension even by those much older. JoJo Rabbit. Written and directed by Taika Waititi. Starring Roman Griffin Davis, Thomasin McKenzie and Scarlett Johansson. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. This review originally appeared in the Post on January 19, 2020 Roman Griffin Davis stars as JoJo and Taiki Waititi as Adolf Hitler.

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Only Yesterday. Movie reeview by Chris Honoré Only Yesterday was written and directed by Isao Takahata who cofounded the iconic Studio Ghibli with Hayao Miyazaki. When released in Japan in 1991 it was a box office sensation, yet, surprisingly, failed to reach the U.S. until 2016. If the works of Miyazaki and Takahata have captured the imaginations of your youngsters, then Only Yesterday is a must see. It’s extraordinary, an example, once again, of the stunning artistry and storytelling that has become the brand of Ghibli. The film’s narrative touches on adult themes while focusing on hybrid protagonists: a 27-year-old woman and a 10-year-old girl. The story begins with Taeko Okajima, a kind of Japanese everywoman, an office worker and life-long resident of Tokyo. She departs by train for a vacation trip in the country to visit relatives, intending to help with the seasonal harvest of safflowers. On her journey while travelling through the night on a sleeper car, headed for the rural town of Yamagata, she begins to reminisce about her childhood: a strict father, puberty, bad grades, first crushes, insecurities, the mockery of mean girls, all told from the point of view of a 10-year-old who is negotiating the 5th grade. These images, beautifully animated and lyrical, are blended seamlessly with the reactions of the older, increasingly reflective Taeko. At one point she says, “I didn’t expect to bring my fifthgrade self along for the trip.” She is met at the Yamagata train station by a young man, Toshio (Dev Patel), a friend of the family, with whom she strikes up a friendship and it’s with him that she begins to share her very personal and conflicted memories. During her stay in this bucolic setting, walking the fields of flowers, enveloped by the soft hillsides, she grows ever more wistful about her past. She reflects on her dreams from childhood, and wonders if the life she is living in Tokyo is truly one she wishes to continue. There is, of course, her growing fondness for Toshio. Only Yesterday is a work of art, wonderfully told, absent intensely imagined, suspend-your-disbelief characters. Instead, the fable moves gently, at times sadly, from the present to the past and back with calm tenderness. Only Yesterday (1991). Written and directed by Isao Takahata. Animé by Studio Ghibli. Voices of Daisey Ridley, Dev Patel and Ashley Eckstein. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG
articles.title: Only Yesterday a must see for kids

articles.text: In search of something novel to do on a recent anniversary, we came across an exhibition of J. M. W. Turner, one of Michael’s favorite painters, born Joseph Mallord William Turner. The Turner exhibit is at the Jacquemart-André Musée, a small gem of a museum among the 130 or so in Paris. This retrospective of Turner’s art comprises 60 watercolors and 10 oil paintings. We spent an enjoyable hour and a half perusing them all, but, “These weren’t Turner’s A-list works,” Michael proclaimed. Drawn entirely from Clore Gallery, the London Tate is the treasure house of Turner’s massive bequest in 1856 to the National Gallery, comprising 300 oils, 30,000 watercolors, and Turner’s 300 sketchbooks. Anyone seeing the film Mr. Turner (2014) starring Timothy Spall, may recall the scenes portraying the artist’s final days amid sprawling stacks of canvases in his enormous day-lit workroom. The Turner exhibit at the Jacquemart-André, on view through late January, is worth a tour of this exquisite Italianate mansion, now a public museum. Serial displays of temporary art collections are open for viewing in the upperfloor gallery. Built under the vast urban project to rid Paris of slums, diseases, and crime, Georges-Eugène Haussmann, or Baron Haussmann as he’s referred to — was Napoleon III’s French official who accomplished, depending on one’s point of view, annihilation of the old city by bulldozing entire districts; or the genius who modernized Paris. “Rectilinear axes were traced out from the périphérique to the city’s center,” which means that streets became linear and boulevards were broadened into throughways. The Jacquemart mansion rose from the razed slums in the brand-new sparkling 8th arrondissement, appropriately near to luxury shopping at Galleries de Lafayette. We exited at the metro, unintentionally one station short of the musée, so we hoofed the extra mile. In clear evidence of Parisians’ love of art, culture, and history, we joined a queue of about a one-hour wait for museum entry. As is typical of city estates, from the street, you don’t have a clue as to how extraordinary and lavish the home behind the arched carriage doors really is. Finally, our turn in line, we walked up a cobbled stone driveway that circled the mansion; and beheld the home’s entry, a showstopper of grandeur with marble carvings and limestone glittering in the sunlight. Children in party dress were engaged in playful banter, and we slowed to linger with other guests as I dreamily envisioned that we had just disembarked from a carriage upon an afternoon garden party. The rooms inside the imposing structure are original, all decked out in 19th Century upper-caste décor. The walls are somberly The Field of Waterloo, oil painting, 1818. The 19th C. influential art critic John Ruskin elevated Turner above his contemporaries for his late in life mastery of watercolor in depicting light, atmosphere, and weather. painted in dense hues; rugs are finely hand-stitched; and every furnishing is ornately fitted with silken fabrics threaded in gold. The weight of its unrelenting richness feels oppressive. I thereby sought to find out who these fine people were. Edouard André was heir to the richest banking family in France. He graduated from Saint Cyr as an officer in the elite corps in protection of Napoleon III. At age 31, he left the military and assumed his father’s seat in the National Assembly and began building his mansion, a project that lasted nearly 10 years. He also enjoyed Parisian life, and the mansion’s 1876 debut was a society phenomenon attracting rave reviews. Cornélie (Nélie) Jacquemart was born into a modest family whose father was in the employ of a wealthy French baron. She was a lively girl with a curious sensibility, and she displayed an early artistic gift for art. The barContinued on next page Upstairs gallery at Musée Jacquemart-André exhibit of J. M. W. Turner in quaint surroundings where the floor creaks under one’s steps on the carpeting. Avon Gorge, 1791, pen, ink, watercolor. Turner (1775 – 1851), the art protégé exhibited from 1790 at the Royal Academy. A Londoner his entire life, he never lost the Cockney accent. One of Turner’s last oil paintings in 1850, La Visite de la Tombe. For an online visit to the Jacquemart exhibit, go to: https://www.museejacquemart-andre.com/sites/default/files/editeur/Pdf/dossier_groupes_ turner.pdf From the street one can’t detect the majesty of the home behind the carriage doors. Edouard André and his wife Nèlie Jacquemart traveled the world collecting art.

articles.text: One of the most important parts of the architecture of any building is the entry, the thing that first orients users and is very important in establishing an overall aesthetic impression. As I walk through Piedmont looking at the homes as well as the civic and commercial buildings, some entries are obvious, welcoming and the focal point of the street architecture. Unfortunately, a few are not so nice – sometimes abrupt and/or even difficult to find. The whole character of the building seems to be set by the entry. What then are some of the things that make for a nice entry? I think the first thing, most importantly, is the location. While certainly not necessary to be formally centered on the home or public building, it should be located in an obvious and primary position, reinforced by the massing and architectural punctuation of the entire entry façade. There should be no confusion as to where to enter. As much as possible the garage and car parking areas should be separate from and architecturally subordinate to the main pedestrian entry – the front door. Secondly, the front door area should have some sort of cover and be protected. This not only home’s appeal. and the softening effect of a second floor over the garage.

articles.text: Supervisor Tom Wilhite and a team of four from Terra Landscape plant a new Southern Magnolia at the Piedmont Center for Arts. The Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia recently received a tree that helps identify its location. On October 15, a new Southern Magnolia was planted at the Center. The new tree replaces a magnolia that had been standing since the early 1930s when the building was constructed by the Wetmore family. The original had begun failing a half-dozen years ago. “That [tree] was one of the crown jewels of the city,” said Sue Malick, president of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “The city did a great job and showed sensitivity in the choice of this new tree. The Center is so grateful to be working with them in such a productive way,” added Sue Malick. Dave Frankel, an arborist, resident, and recently retired from the City as Public Works Supervisor had observed the slow decline of the former magnolia over the last decade. The tips of the branches were experiencing “dieback” - the progressive death of twigs, shoots, and branches from the tip downward. “I thought the city’s decision to take down the tree was very appropriate,” Frankel affirmed. Tom Wilhite, Construction Manager for Terra Landscape, the firm with a contract to maintain all the city’s parks and public spaces, explained the attributes of Piedmont’s newest tree, “That felty texture and rust color on The previous magnolia at the Center for the Arts was on its last legs, with roughly one-third of the tree dying. The new tree magnolia likes rich, moist, well-drained soil and could reach full size in 20 years. It is fast-growing and has begun to bloom at a young age. the underside of the leaves is highly desirable. This is a 36” box tree, which is a large tree to transplant.” This tree came from Boething Treeland in Portola Valley, not far from Palo Alto, so one might consider it a Stanford tree. “This South Magnolia’s particular cultivar is called ‘Samuel Sommer.’ Its beautiful white flowers are the largest of any Southern Magnolia cultivar; they can reach 14 inches across,” Wilhite said with a smile. Samuel Sommers types are half the size of other Southern Magnolias, growing 30-40 feet tall with a 30-foot wide canopy. They can live for up to 150 years. This tree (not yet named) has an excellent chance to thrive, Wilhite noted that the location was ideal because of its “sunny but somewhat protected place.” He and his team from Terra amended the soil with organic and mineral components and starter fertilizer. A berm was installed by the base as were two “bubblers” to ensure deep irrigation.
articles.title: Center for the Arts receives new Magnolia tree

articles.text: Several years ago, I had the opportunity to visit the sherry producing region at the southern tip of Spain. My knowledge before the trip was somewhat limited – all I knew was that I loved a cold glass of fino sherry as an aperitif. When I got there, I discovered there was huge range of sherries that go from bone dry to immensely sweet. Sherry starts life as wine until someone dramatically interrupts it with a heaping serving of high-ABV neutral grain spirit. Not only does the spirit lift sherry’s alcohol level, it kills off any remaining yeast, stopping fermentation. But for sherry, that’s just the beginning. What really defines sherry is the way it’s aged: the different types are basically expressions of the science (and some slightly frustrating magic) of aging. mend a stop in the freezer for 15 minutes. It has a nose of lemony citrus and is clean and refreshing on the palate. The driest liquid you will ever taste. Serve with a hard Spanish cheese, like Manchego. • Gonzalez Byass Vina AB Amontillado, $25 Amontillado Sherries are a step up in intensity and weight from Fino Sherry. This one was aged 12 years in the solera and has a complex nose with strong aromatics, rosemary and thyme covering the roasted nuts, bitter oranges and curry. The medium-to-full-bodied palate shows a very spicy smoky wine with hints of coffee, layered, intense and subtle. All Sherry is aged with the Solera system – basically a cask-rotation system where the final product is a blend of younger and older sherries. But while some sherries are oxidized—meaning allowed exposure to oxygen, which impacts the flavor—some are intentionally deprived, kept under a naturally occurring (and systematically encouraged) layer of yeast called a “flor,” basically a club bouncer for oxygen trying to get into the party. Because the flor comes from ambient yeast in the winery, where sherry is aged becomes part of its expression. When the flor disappears, on purpose or by accident (see below), oxidation occurs and darker, richer flavors arise. That is one reason why sherry can achieve the incredible hoodwink of having a sweet, fruity, nutty aroma and a bone-dry mouthfeel. It also makes it great for food pairing and in cocktails. One of the regrets after my trip to Spain was that I did not have time to visit some important producers, one of which was Gonzales Byass. So, I was delighted to recently have the opportunity to taste the range of Gonzalez Byass Sherries. This outstanding producer was founded in 1835 and is one of the most venerated producers in Spain. Lucky for us, the wines are well distributed in the U.S. and are available in many Bay Area stores. For further information contact Donna White Communications. • Tio Pepe Fino Sherry, $20 This is probably the most famous dry sherry in America. Technically it is a fortified wine but at 15% alcohol it is not much stronger than a regular wine. The resulting Sherry combines the crisp, dry, delicate flavors of a Fino or Amontillado with the richness of Oloroso. This one is mostly dry and nutty with just a touch of sweetness. A very satisfying dram. • Gonzalez Byass Alfonso Oloroso Seco, $25 Olorosos come in both sweet and dry styles and this one is definitely dry. articles.text: Shopping by appointment starts October 25th The Bookmark Bookstore, operated by the nonprofit Friends of the Oakland Public Library, recently announced another way to shop for quality used books. The Bookmark is now accepting reservations for in-store shopping. Customers can make a reservation on the store website. “We are thrilled to welcome our customers back for live shopping using our new reservation system,” exclaimed Friends volunteer. With a $10 deposit, customers get to browse the store for 45 minutes. The deposit will be applied to purchases made at the Bookmark. Each 45-minute reservation may be used for one or two adults, plus children under 18. Safety is the Bookmark’s highest priority and customers are required to follow a few simple rules for the safety of customers, volunteers, and staff. Safety measures include wearing a mask, observing social distancing protocols, and use of hand sanitizer before entering the store. All the details of in-store shopping and the link to make a reservation are available on the website at https://www.fopl. org/bookmark-reservations. For customers who are not comfortable shopping in person or can’t find a time that work for their schedule, the Virtual Bookstore is a great option for shopping anytime: https://www.fopl.org/ virtual-bookstore. Books waiting to be purchased at the Bookmark Bookstore in Old Town Oakland await knowing buyers. The Bookmark Bookstore is located in Old Oakland, at 721 Washington Street. Modified store hours for in-store shopping reservations and curbside pickup are Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. All purchases support the Oakland Public Library.
articles.title: The Bookmark Bookstore – supporting Oakland Pubic Library

articles.text: To get a book from the library these days, you simply go online to the library site and check what’s there. If you want to search for new books, there is a brief video tutorial showing how to do that: https://oaklandlibrary.org/blogs/from-main-library/ oakand-public-library-launches-playlist-help-you-find-newbooks-and-more. It was posted by librarian Rebekah Eppley last month. Find what you want? Request it and wait for an email confirmation that tells when and where you can come get it. At Piedmont Avenue branch, the pick-up hours are 10 to 1 Tuesday through Saturday. The service is outdoors. You’ll find tables arranged to keep a safe distance between staff and patrons. Go up to the table and show your library card to the masked librarian. She/he calls on a walkie-talkie to someone inside the library and in a few minutes your books are brought out in a paper bag with your name on it.
articles.title: Sidewalk pickup at the library

articles.text: Dorothy Lazard, the Librarian at the Oakland History Center, usually hosts a series of events at the Main Library in the Fall. articles.text: Lake Merritt at night. I am pleased to announce that The Lake Merritt has secured a very coveted speaker for our Topics of Merritt program on Tuesday, November 10, 2020 at 1:00 p.m. Damon Tighe, a Naturalist at the California Center for Natural History and Biotechnology, and Educator at Bio-Rad Laboratories, will present a free Zoom program for residents at The Lake Merritt. The event is open to all. Based in Oakland, Tighe has become acclaimed for his work documenting the spectacular marine organisms thriving beneath the surface of Lake Merritt. His dramatic underwater photographs and compelling stories reveal the history of these stunning life forms, many from around the world, who have found a home in Lake Merritt. Did you know that Lake Merritt is not a man-made lake, but a tidal lagoon that formed 10,000 years ago in the Neolithic era? At that time, rising sea levels carried water from the Pacific Ocean inland and a tidal lagoon formed in what is now Downtown Oakland. The lagoon was connected to the Bay by a large rivulet that carried a steady stream of saltwater and wildlife inland from the ocean. Fresh water from winter rains runs down our hills through many creeks and into the lake, creating a mixed brackish environment suitable for many marine creatures then and now. Over the decades Tighe has kept a watchful eye on the creatures living in the lake. After getting reports over several years in a row from boaters on the lake concerning a beautiful soft blue glow around their oars at night, Tighe investigated. His research resulted in a very compelling article in Bay Nature magazine. “Why Is Lake Merritt Turning Photo by Chris Hitchcock Blue at Night?” explains the phenomenon. Tighe’s research discovered that during the summer months when the creeks run dry, the salinity of the lake’s water rises to become much more like that of the Bay. Coinciding with this change in salinity, a bloom in marine organisms begins in the shallow warm waters. By late summer and early fall, the microscopic organisms responsible for the blue glow, a plankton called dinoflagellates, erupt and multiply. After reading an article about Tighe in The Oaklandside this past July, I was intrigued by some of his other discoveries. The citizen scientist knows the lake and its environs well. He steps around picnickers, turns over rocks on the shore, and even wades through the water, his eyes alert for the smallest marine critters. To date, more than 600 species have been identified at Lake Merritt, including non-native life forms and some that are so unique that they have not been found anywhere else on Earth. The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Community sits directly across from the lake. I have spent many an hour walking along the lake noticing the plants and wildlife, but never imagined what was under the water. To hear more, the public is invited to a webinar on Tuesday, November 10 at 1:00 p.m. Admission to this Zoom presentation is free, but reservations are required. To obtain a link for this webinar, email rsvp@thelakemerrittsenior. com or call 510-903-3600. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street in Oakland. For further information call 510- 903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com. pages.text: Wednesday, October 21, 2020 25 Seniors How to know you are being scammed By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I am a photographer. I just got an email from someone who wants to hire me for an outdoor wedding here in Oakland. He told me the date and asked for my fee. I told him that it depends on what he wants me to shoot, how many prints he wants, etc. , and suggested that we speak by phone. He asked for a ballpark figure which I gave him, and then I suggested again that he give me his phone number so we could speak on the phone. He emailed me back and said that his friend had offered to pay for my services as a wedding present. He never gave me his phone number, and then yesterday, I got a check for way over the fee that I gave him from some flooring company in Oklahoma. He then emailed me and asked if I received the check. This seems fishy! Is this a scam? Bart G.., Oakland Dear Bart: You are absolutely right. This is a kind of scam called a “fake check” scam. There are many ways that this can take form, but this request for your services, and then an overpayment is one that has been going around lately. As a matter of fact, some of you know that I am a professional musician as well as the MacMama. I received a very similar email last month, from somebody who wanted me to play violin at a wedding in Berkeley and asked about my fee. It’s almost exactly the same as the email you received. This person must have seen my website and reached out to me with details that would make me less likely to suspect his behavior. When I told him my fee, and said we should speak on the phone, he ignored me. And last week, I received a check for $1900, on a very flimsy piece of paper that looked fake. But these checks often get through the bank, according to the FTC “… because fake checks generally look just like real checks, even to bank employees. They are often printed with the names and addresses of legitimate financial institutions. They may even be real checks written on bank accounts that belong to identity theft victims. It can take weeks for a bank to figure out that the check is a fake. By law, banks have to make deposited funds available quickly, usually within two days. When the funds are made available in your account, the bank may say the check has “cleared,” but that doesn’t mean it’s a good check. Fake checks can take weeks to be discovered and untangled. By that time, the scammer has any money you sent, and you’re stuck paying the money back to the bank. Your best bet: Don’t rely on money from a check unless you know and trust the person you’re dealing with.” Since you are a photographer, with a website that probably has contact information, and even your office address (I have since removed my address from my websites), the scammer does not even need to pry that information out of you. And the fact that they did not ask the usual questions someone asks when hiring a photographer (or in my case a musician) for a wedding is a tip off. The use of an overpayment with a fake check is one of the most common tools. Often times, they claim that they sent the wrong check and want you to pay it back, sometimes even threatening you. But there are other ways that scammers trick folks out of thousands of dollars, sometimes contacting victims by phone, but more and more by email. I have heard from several self-employed contractors this month who have received emails like the one you received, with almost identical wording. Often times, these are folks who get a few hundred to a few thousand dollars, and then disappear. These days, credit card companies are getting savvy to fraudulent charges, so the scammers are finding other ways to steal from unsuspecting victims. articles.text: In an all-Piedmont wedding, Elizabeth Chapple Faughnan (PHS ’08) and Daniel Scott Davis (PHS ’06) were married on September 12, 2020. The ceremony and reception were held among the redwoods at the Sonoma County property that has been in Libby’s family for over 50 years. The Honorable Kathleen A. Kelly, Judge for the Superior Court of San Francisco County and a close friend of the bride’s family, acted as officiant. Although Libby and Dan grew up less than a mile apart, they did not formally meet until attending college at UC Davis. Both are graduates of Piedmont High School, UC Davis and Samuel Merritt University, where they completed the Accelerated Bachelor of Science in Nursing. Libby also earned her Master of Science in Nursing—Family Nurse Practitioner degree at Samuel Merritt. Dan is an RN in the Intensive Care Unit at the Alta Bates Summit Medical Center, and Libby is an RN in the Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital Family Birth Center. Libby is the daughter of Vincent and Claire Faughnan and the granddaughter of James and Suzanne Soper, all of Piedmont, and the granddaughter of Vincent and Catherine Faughnan of New York. Dan is the son of Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado of Piedmont and the grandson of Herbert and Viella Jean Davis of Denver, Colorado, and the grandson of Juan de Jesus Alvarado and Ana Paula Sanchez de Alvarado of Caracas, Venezuela. Libby and Dan became engaged in October 2019 and started planning a large wedding to be held on September 12, 2020. Libby Faughnan and Dan Davis, both of Piedmont, were married on September 12 in Sonoma County. They did not let the coronavirus or California wildfires cancel their plans. They reduced their wedding guest list to an immediate family group of 12. The week they got married included days of dark, smoky skies and a day when the sun appeared blood-orange all day. Their wedding day was hazy but happy and the entire group was grateful to celebrate together. The bride and groom are planning a honeymoon in Hawaii in 2021.
articles.title: Libby Faughnan marries Dan Davis on September 12

articles.text: Lucretia Crandall Wieking, a longtime former Piedmont resident, passed away at home in Chico surrounded by her family on October 14, 2020. She was 87. Born on January 20, 1933 in Berkeley, California, she was the daughter of Giles and Lucile Crandall. She lived most of her life in Piedmont and the East Bay before moving to Chico in recent years to be closer to her family. She attended school at Havens Elementary in Piedmont, and Anna Head School in Oakland before enrolling at UC Berkeley. While at Cal she was a member of the Alpha Phi Sorority. She cherished her many beloved friends from her school days and continued those friendships throughout her life. She married James Potter Wieking on October 15, 1954. A stay-at-home mother and wife, she was her family’s rock and championed their lives. She felt her family was her greatest accomplishment. Her favorites in life were here family, her dear friends, sports, playing bridge, and her many treasured pets. She took joy in visiting the Oakland Zoo. She was a sports fan of the Cal Bears and Raiders football teams, and she frequently watched golf and mored way. She was known to say, “a little dirt won’t hurt”. Most recently she summed up her life in simple terms: “She came, she lived, she left”. Lucretia was a member of the Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland, the Junior Center of Arts and Science, and was a sustaining member of the Junior League of Oakland. She is survived by Jim Wieking, her husband of 66 years, and her brother, and sister-in-law Sheldon and Janet Crandall of Piedmont. She is also survived by daughter Linda Catalano and husband Tony, and son Edward Wieking. She is additionally survived by two grandchildren, Daniel James McDonald and Kinsey McDonald Gilbert (Danny Ray), by great-granddaughter Marie Gilbert, as well as numerous nieces and nephews. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations be made to the Oakland Zoo, Guide Dogs for the Blind in San Rafael, or any other animal welfare organization or charity of your choice. A private family celebration of her life will be held at a later date. To view online and leave condolences for the family, go to www. NewtonBracewell.com. Born on January 20, 1933 in Berkeley, California, she was the daughter of Giles and Lucile Crandall. She lived most of her life in Piedmont and the East Bay before moving to Chico in recent years to be closer to her family. She attended school at Havens Elementary in Piedmont, and Anna Head School in Oakland before enrolling at UC Berkeley. While at Cal she was a member of the Alpha Phi Sorority. She cherished her many beloved friends from her school days and continued those friendships throughout her life. She married James Potter Wieking on October 15, 1954. A stay-at-home mother and wife, she was her family’s rock and championed their lives. She felt her family was her greatest accomplishment. Her favorites in life were here family, her dear friends, sports, playing bridge, and her many treasured pets. She took joy in visiting the Oakland Zoo. She was a sports fan of the Cal Bears and Raiders football teams, and she frequently watched golf and mored way. She was known to say, “a little dirt won’t hurt”. Most recently she summed up her life in simple terms: “She came, she lived, she left”. Lucretia was a member of the Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland, the Junior Center of Arts and Science, and was a sustaining member of the Junior League of Oakland. She is survived by Jim Wieking, her husband of 66 years, and her brother, and sister-in-law Sheldon and Janet Crandall of Piedmont. What are the estimated costs of the project compared to bond revenues and what steps will the City take to limit project costs to available bond revenues? The measure would authorize the City to issue bonds with a principal value that does not exceed $19.5 million. In the event the City receives an AA+ bond rating, it is conceivable the bonds would be sold at a premium and Measure UU would provide revenues in excess of the face value of the bonds. The City determined that the $19.5 million figure was appropriate based on rough “hard cost” estimates as follows: $8 million for the two pools to replace the current “medium” and “big” pools, $3.5 million for site preparation, and $6 million for a building to house the pool equipment, restrooms, offices, and community space. If necessary, the concept can be value-engineered during final design development to meet the budget parameters. 9. Can the City repair the existing pool? The City has determined that repairing the existing pool is not a feasible option. The City has been continuously repairing the existing pool since it took over operations in 2011. The repairs required to keep the facility safe and operational have become increasingly expensive every year, and the facility is now at the point where pool decks need to be removed in order to address structural issues. A renovation of the existing facility would require not only major structural repair and equipment replacement, but would also trigger significant site work required to meet current health, safety, and accessibility regulations. 10. What oversight is in place to ensure that the bond funds are used properly? Measure UU provides that a bond oversight committee be appointed to make sure the bonds are issued and spent in accordance with the terms of Measure UU. As with any project, staff and the City Council will also work to ensure proper use of public funds. The project will also be subject to the City’s project risk management policy.

articles.text: We all know there comes a time when it no longer makes economic sense to spend money on something too broken to fix. For the Piedmont Pool, that time has come. Our old pool leaks over one million gallons of water a year from somewhere underneath the deck. The only way to fix the leaking is to rip out and replace the concrete, which would cost millions of tax dollars. Even if the City had funds to replace the deck, which it doesn’t, the unreliable and inefficient 56-year-old pool mechanics would remain. Replacing the deck would be like replacing an old car’s exterior, and hoping the unreliable gas guzzling engine can keep going a few more miles. When we’re spending millions of tax dollars, this makes no sense. If Piedmont is going to have a community pool, it’s time to build a new one. It has been apparent for decades that the city didn’t have a big enough pool to accommodate the many residents who would like to use it for sports, recreation, and exercise. In addition to better meeting resident needs, a new pool will provide a better community gathering place. It will be a place where we can have teen lifeguards supervising toddlers taking swimming lessons, have our high school chemistry teacher coaching the HS water polo team, have adults rehabbing from an injury, and have seniors lap swimming, all at the same time. There is no other facility that brings all members of our community together in such a way from the dead of winter to the hottest summer days. Sure, rebuilding a pool the same size as the current pool would be less expensive, but it would continue to exclude many families and it would still require the schools to spend tens of thousands of dollars to rent pool space elsewhere. When the School District rebuilt Havens and other school buildings, the community saw this as an opportunity to make these shared spaces materially better and strengthen our sense of community. Our contemplated investment in the Piedmont community pool is no different. Piedmonters do their homework, are well-informed about the issues, and are generous in their commitment to maintaining what’s great about our city. Investing in a new community pool for everyone to enjoy is the right decision for our community, our property values, and our stewardship for future generations. Let’s show our kids what it means to take care of the community we love, by rebuilding the community pool. Please join me in voting Yes on Measure UU. Jen Cavenaugh is a member of Piedmont City Council

articles.text: Editor: I am a full-time working mom of three kids aged 6, 4, and 1.5. The amazing resources for working parents in this town — walkable neighborhood schools, easy access to great after-school activities — are a significant reason my family bought our house here in 2015. The pool factored into this calculation as well. Water safety is crucial, and it would be hard for my family to find time to drive kids to Alameda or Lafayette on a regular basis for swim lessons. My family, and many similarly situated families, place a high value on the ease of a nearby community pool for both lessons and just plain fun. I have no idea at this point if any of my children will be interested in competitive swimming, but I also very much hope they will at least have the opportunity to participate in local club and school swim teams without the potentially complicated logistics of practicing in rented space in other towns. We are an aff luent, kidfriendly suburban California community. It would be senseless to shutter our pool for good. Fundamentally, I also believe that investment in facilities for the common good of the community is worthy and important. The current pool has lasted for 56 years. Piedmont residents now have the opportunity to invest in a new facility that will support the schools and benefit the entire community for decades to come. I hope others will join me in voting Yes on Measure UU. –Amanda Straub
articles.title: Investment for common good of community is worthy

articles.text: Measure UU is not about me, and it’s not about today. I’m voting Yes on UU because it’s in the best long-term interests of our city, our community, and our neighbors – present and future. It’s for my friends next door, whose two young boys will learn to swim there. It’s for the young kids who will have fond memories of their birthday parties there like my family did. It’s for my elderly neighbor across the street; he can’t run, but he can still swim. It’s for the teenager who finds solace and belonging in water polo. It’s for the future homebuyers who see this facility as the centerpiece of our vibrant and verdant community. The time is now. We cannot wait. I hope you join me in improving our community today, and for generations to come, by voting Yes on UU. –Aaron J. Aubrecht
articles.title: Measure UU is long-term investment of city

articles.text: About 55 years ago my parents joined the Piedmont Swim Club. My mother loved swimming and wanted to make sure all seven of her children could swim. My siblings and I participated on the swim team; became lifeguards, swim instructors and water polo coaches. I was also the pool manager after college and, last year, a swim instructor again. The pool wasn’t just the place where we learned to swim; we became part of the larger Piedmont aquatic community. It helped foster a love for swimming and water polo that we passed on to our children. We found our passion. During summers the Piedmont pool lifeguard staff was primarily Piedmont high school students and the swim program instructors were PHS graduates home from college. It became a reunion of swim team and swim club friends and classmates. It was fun to see the progress in students from one year to the next. Parents knew the colleges the guards and instuctors attended, even giving some good-natured ribbing about rival schools. We were a large family. Over the years working at the pool I saw firsthand the importance of having a pool in the center of town. People needed the pool for a variety of reasons: recovering from surgery, dealing with back issues, fighting through MS. My own mother needed the pool as she fought her cancer. The staff and other swimmers knew each of them by name; encouraged them during their workout and missed them when they were gone. When I started swimming back at the pool again with a masters team, I met Christine, Bev and others. We pushed each other through workouts and complained about the parts we didn’t like. We were friends through swimming. Having a pool in Piedmont is so important. It is a place where a child can gain self-esteem through swimming or water polo. It is a place where you find new friends who have a shared passion for swimming. It is a place where our youth can get their first job. It is a place where our high school and college students can be role models as teachers. It is a place where you find passion for aquatics; you can foster friendships. It is a place where you find our true community. Please support Measure UU. Megan Finney Hernandez is a former member of the U.S. Water Polo team.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 21, 2020 29 Piedmont Pool too broken to be fixed By Jennifer Cavenaugh We all know there comes a time when it no longer makes economic sense to spend money on something too broken to fix. For the Piedmont Pool, that time has come. Our old pool leaks over one million gallons of water a year from somewhere underneath the deck. The only way to fix the leaking is to rip out and replace the concrete, which would cost millions of tax dollars. Even if the City had funds to replace the deck, which it doesn’t, the unreliable and inefficient 56-year-old pool mechanics would remain. Replacing the deck would be like replacing an old car’s exterior, and hoping the unreliable gas guzzling engine can keep going a few more miles. When we’re spending millions of tax dollars, this makes no sense. If Piedmont is going to have a community pool, it’s time to build a new one. It has been apparent for decades that the city didn’t have a big enough pool to accommodate the many residents who would like to use it for sports, recreation, and exercise. In addition to better meeting resident needs, a new pool will provide a better community gathering place. It will be a place where we can have teen lifeguards supervising toddlers taking swimming lessons, have our high school chemistry teacher coaching the HS water polo team, have adults rehabbing from an injury, and have seniors lap swimming, all at the same time. There is no other facility that brings all members of our community together in such a way from the dead of winter to the hottest summer days. Sure, rebuilding a pool the same size as the current pool would be less expensive, but it would continue to exclude many families and it would still require the schools to spend tens of thousands of dollars to rent pool space elsewhere. When the School District rebuilt Havens and other school buildings, the community saw this as an opportunity to make these shared spaces materially better and strengthen our sense of community. Our contemplated investment in the Piedmont community pool is no different. Piedmonters do their homework, are well-informed about the issues, and are generous in their commitment to maintaining what’s great about our city. Investing in a new community pool for everyone to enjoy is the right decision for our community, our property values, and our stewardship for future generations. Let’s show our kids what it means to take care of the community we love, by rebuilding the community pool. Please join me in voting Yes on Measure UU. articles.text: No easing of restrictions by County after moving to Orange Tier Three new cases of COVID- 19 were recorded in Piedmont in the past week, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department yesterday, Tuesday, October 20. In total, 41 cases have been reported in Piedmont since the coronavirus outbreak in March. Overall, the caseload in Alameda County is 22,807 as of yesterday. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for tests in the county is 1.4 percent, slightly lower than earlier in the month. One person in Piedmont died since last Tuesday, October 13. The county has now recorded 432 total COVID-19 fatalities. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 8,888. In Hayward, 3,364 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,562 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,242. Last week, state health officials proclaimed that Alameda County has been placed in a less-restrictive Orange Tier for reopening its economy amid the ongoing coronavirus pandemic. The Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, is the second-least restrictive tier of the state’s four-tiered color-coded system. However, county officials are proceeding with caution and keeping restrictions tighter than required by the state. The county said it will update current health orders next week. On Thursday, October 15, the county provided guidance for how to reopen some performing arts and fine arts sectors. San Francisco County was moved into the least restrictive Yellow Tier, or Minimal Tier, this week. It is the only Bay Area county to achieve that. Alameda County was in the most restrictive Purple Tier when the system was launched in August, then moved into the second-most restrictive Red Tier last month. Due to decreasing case and positivity rates, Alameda County is now one of 23 counties in the two least restrictive tiers, Orange and Yellow. According to the state, Orange Tier counties can allow for indoor dining, indoor religious services and indoor theaters, but with strict capacity limits. Capacity limits for indoor retail and shopping malls can be increased to 50 percent in Orange Tier counties. In California, 874,077 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded, and there have been 16,992 deaths due to the disease. The City of Piedmont last week echoed guidance from the county noting that trick-or-treating this Halloween is considered a high-risk activity and is not recommended. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host its citywide Climate Challenge next month, following the success of last year’s Climate Challenge. In 2019, more than 250 Piedmont households answered the call to be more environmentally-conscience through different challenges that aimed to reduce the city’s collective greenhouse gas emissions by over 200 tons. This year, the goals will be set even higher. The City has announced its intention to double the number of participating households, from 250 to 500 sign-ups, by Earth Day, April 22, 2021. In addition, a goal has been set to reduce Piedmont’s carbon emissions by 500 tons. The Climate Challenge gives residents the chance to participate in teams and community organizations, and to engage in some friendly competition to see which household can reduce their carbon footprint the most. Residents can use the platform to learn more about their household’s emissions, and to plan lifestyle changes that will positively affect their impact on the environment. The City is encouraging residents who signed up for the challenge last year to continue to engage with it this year. New actions and challenges have been added for this year’s challenge. The challenge will run from November 2020 to May 2021. Residents can sign up for the challenge at: https://www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org/. On that website residents can create a profile for their household and pledge to commit to adopt sustainable actions that help reduce their carbon footprint. Those actions will be added to your dashboard, and the platform will help with next steps, costs, and questions. “This is a fun, meaningful way to work towards a shared decrease in Piedmont emissions. The vast majority of emissions in Piedmont stem from households, and using this website brings attention to this fact and helps us all be more sustainable,” said Nate Redinbo, the Planning Department’s new Climate Fellow. articles.text: Just like everything in 2020, Halloween is going to look a little different, too. But before you give up on the fun of running to and from your neighbors’ doors, check out the new Halloween game in town! For two weeks, from October 17 to Halloween, Saturday, October 31, Piedmont BOO will allow kids to celebrate Halloween. It’s a fun, socially distanced, reverse trick or treat game for kids of all ages. Instead of ringing doorbells for candy, you choose a location from a map provided to participants, gather a few tricks and treats to share. and leave them on your neighbor’s doorstep, sneaking off unseen just like a ghost. That’s why it’s called a BOO! It’s also a fundraiser for schools with all proceeds going directly to the Piedmont Education Foundation. When you sign up to join the fun at www. piedmontstore.org, you’ll add your address to the Piedmont BOO participation list. Pick up your yard sign and BOO Count stickers from one of the drive-by pickup locations, gather some $25 for Piedmont BOO! Kit. It includes a lawn sign, three BOO count stickers and access to the address list for the game $50 for the WHOLE BOO Kit. This includes a lawn sign, three BOO count stickers, access to the address list, plus 3 complete BOO bags filled with treats and ready for giving. Fundraising for Piedmont schools has never been so much fun. Proceeds from this “reverse trick-or-treating” game will go to the Piedmont Education Foundation. Halloween goodies to share and choose three locations to deliver your spooky offerings to from the participant list or from Piedmont BOO signs in your neighborhood. Then slip over and leave an anonymous gift or treat on their doorstep. They’ve now been BOOed (distinctly different from ball games), and after adding a sticker to their yard sign to let everyone know they’ve gotten one of their three Halloween surprises, they’re off to choose their three houses to treat. Kids of all ages are welcome to play, whether age two or 80. To limit risk factors, you need to sign up to play so there’s a record of participants for safety. Piedmont BOO wants to see the whole town enjoying themselves by sharing their Halloween spirit with each other in a safe, socially-distanced way. Treats don’t need to be big. Grab a spooky bag or basket and fill it with your choice of Halloween surprises. Halloween crafts, small toys or games and packaged treats are always fun! Slime, small decorations and gift cards are also great options. Candy, of course, but be allergy aware in your choices by bagging chocolate and/or nut candies in separate Ziploc bags. To participate without putting a BOO basket together, choose “The Whole BOO!” option at piedmontstore.org and you can pick up three pre-filled BOO bags ready for gifting when you get your yard sign and BOO count stickers.
articles.title: Piedmont BOO: a socially-distanced, spooky celebration for kids

articles.text: To make autumn a little more festive, the Piedmont Arts Fund and Piedmont Makers are putting on a socially-distanced scarecrow community art and maker event. Families and pods are invited to make scarecrows for their front yards. This year’s theme is California Dreaming, because we could all use a little optimism and creative cheer. To participate, make a scarecrow with your family or pod and have it in your front yard by Saturday, October 24. Post a picture of your scarecrow on your Facebook or Instagram page and tag #PiedmontScarecrowWalk2020. The Piedmont Arts Fund and Piedmont Makers will be posting scarecrows on their Instagram and Facebook pages. Play Scarecrow Bingo with your family Print out the Scarecrow Bingo card that will be posted on Sunday, October 26. Then take a Scarecrow Walk through Piedmont and fill out your card. Bring your completed card to Mulberry’s Market between October 26 and October 31 to receive a Scarecrow treat (limit one per person). How to make a Scarecrow Piedmont Makers can help. Need some inspiration on design? The Piedmont Arts Fund has some scarecrow inspiration on their website: https://piedmontartsfund.org/upcoming-events/ scarecrowwalk. Have an old Scarecrow in the basement? If you have an old scarecrow in your garage or basement, pull it out, dust it off, and give it a little California spirit. Everyone is welcome to participate. Scarecrows are popping up everywhere this year.
articles.title: Community invited to make scarecrows for Halloween

articles.text: Waldo Avenue, one of Piedmont’s shortest streets and located in the middle of town, has a reputation for being one of the most popular streets for trick or treating on Halloween. Due to concerns about the coronavirus, the Waldonians decided this year to keep the lights off and not host trick or treating – “a sad but safe decision for all,” commented resident Mary Margaret Sinnema. For the past few years Waldo Avenue has had nearly 900 kids come through. The best advice is for families to put Waldo on their list of Halloween activities for October 2021, but not this year.
articles.title: No trick or treating on Waldo this year

articles.text: Dear Piedmonters, Before you vote on Measure UU, we thought there were a few things we needed to tell you. We did tell you that the City has no outstanding General Obligation Bonds, but we didn’t mention that we have LOTS of debts - $7 million in sewer loans, $13 million in Post Employment Benefits Payable, and $26 million in Pension Benefits Payable. Oh, and if our pension portfolio returns only 6.15% instead of the estimated 7.15% (you can get 7.15% on your investments in today’s crazy market with bonds yielding close to zero, can’t you?), our Pension Benefit Liability alone increases to over $43 million. Speaking of deficits, did we mention that our General Fund – that is, unrestricted money that the City can spend on anything – has a deficit of about $9 million? We also glossed over the fact that the ordinance we passed estimates that the total cost of the “improvements” is $23 million, but that it allows us to issue $19.5 million in bonds. Guess who is paying for the difference? We also haven’t mentioned it, but by reading the City Council minutes for the last six months, you can see that we know about the major deficiencies in our ability to deliver essential public services – the Police Chief, Fire Chief, and City Administrator are all on the record as saying that we do not comply with the Essential Services Act, that the fire station may sustain major damage in an earthquake, and that it may cost up to $51 million to fix these problems. That’s why we are looking at creating a Community Facilities District (aka Mello-Roos) to make it easier to issue bonds backed by another special tax on Piedmont homeowners in the near future. And because we generally ask for the maximum amount, it will probably be for the full $51 million. Finally, we haven’t mentioned that 100% of Piedmont citizens rely on our Police and Fire Departments, while an estimated 25% of citizens use the pool. So, if we had placed two bond measures on the November ballot - $50 million for Police and Fire, and $20 million for a new pool, we knew what would happen. Citizens would vote to maintain essential services, but they would turn down the pool. After spending $56 million in 2006 and another $66 million in 2016 on School District Bonds (all that money is gone, and they still haven’t finished their projects), $10 million per year on Measure G, $2.6 million per year on Measure H, and $2.4 million per year on Measure T, citizens are getting a little tax weary. After all, aren’t our property tax rates some of the highest in California? So, think carefully before you vote on measure UU. We’ll see you soon with our new $51 million bond request. You will HAVE to vote yes to maintain city services, but you can vote NO on Measure UU.

pages.text: The Measure UU Letter From the City Council That We Should Have Received Dear Piedmonters, Before you vote on Measure UU, we thought there were a few things we needed to tell you. We did tell you that the City has no outstanding General Obligation Bonds, but we didn’t mention that we have LOTS of debts - $7 million in sewer loans, $13 million in Post Employment Benefits Payable, and $26 million in Pension Benefits Payable. Oh, and if our pension portfolio returns only 6.15% instead of the estimated 7.15% (you can get 7.15% on your investments in today’s crazy market with bonds yielding close to zero, can’t you?), our Pension Benefit Liability alone increases to over $43 million. Speaking of deficits, did we mention that our General Fund – that is, unrestricted money that the City can spend on anything – has a deficit of about $9 million? We also glossed over the fact that the ordinance we passed estimates that the total cost of the “improvements” is $23 million, but that it allows us to issue $19.5 million in bonds. Guess who is paying for the difference? We also haven’t mentioned it, but by reading the City Council minutes for the last six months, you can see that we know about the major deficiencies in our ability to deliver essential public services – the Police Chief, Fire Chief, and City Administrator are all on the record as saying that we do not comply with the Essential Services Act, that the fire station may sustain major damage in an earthquake, and that it may cost up to $51 million to fix these problems. That’s why we are looking at creating a Community Facilities District (aka Mello-Roos) to make it easier to issue bonds backed by another special tax on Piedmont homeowners in the near future. And because we generally ask for the maximum amount, it will probably be for the full $51 million. Finally, we haven’t mentioned that 100% of Piedmont citizens rely on our Police and Fire Departments, while an estimated 25% of citizens use the pool. So, if we had placed two bond measures on the November ballot - $50 million for Police and Fire, and $20 million for a new pool, we knew what would happen. Citizens would vote to maintain essential services, but they would turn down the pool. After spending $56 million in 2006 and another $66 million in 2016 on School District Bonds (all that money is gone, and they still haven’t finished their projects), $10 million per year on Measure G, $2.6 million per year on Measure H, and $2.4 million per year on Measure T, citizens are getting a little tax weary. After all, aren’t our property tax rates some of the highest in California? So, think carefully before you vote on measure UU. We’ll see you soon with our new $51 million bond request. You will HAVE to vote yes to maintain city services, but you can vote NO on Measure UU.
